sources.title: Shaan Puri on persuasion, the ABC goal framework, moving to the right soil, and defining your own success
sources.originalTitle: 9 Harsh Truths No One Wants To Admit - Shaan Puri
sources.outlet: Chris Williamson and My First Million
sources.summary: Shaan covers selling to human nature without being manipulative, simplifying goals into A (where you are), B (next step), Z (the outcome), and why most advice-seeking is really permission-seeking. He argues location, obsession and playfulness matter more than grind, and that success should be balanced rather than extreme.

principles.text: Sell what people actually want, not what they should want; market benefits and a story, and use that understanding for a noble cause.
principles.quote: Never has more money been lost than selling somebody what they should want versus what they do want.

principles.text: When two options both look bad (manipulative vs. ineffective-virtuous), don't debate them; build a third that pairs human psychology with a good cause.
principles.quote: you marry an understanding of human psychology. Hey, people like stories. I should frame what I do in the form of a story.

principles.text: Cure overthinking with ABC: know only where you are (A), the next incremental action (B), and the fixed end goal (Z), then repeat.
principles.quote: you only need to know three letters in the alphabet. A, B, Z. A is where you're currently at.

principles.text: Most requests for advice are really requests for permission; the real gates in life are courage, action and wisdom, not intelligence.
principles.quote: the world is courage gated. It's action gated. It's wisdom gated.

principles.text: Environment is leverage: move to the white-hot center of your interest, because proximity to similar people beats any book or podcast.
principles.quote: Proximity is power.

principles.text: Extreme success has a steep hidden price; define winning for yourself as results plus balance, not the final 10% at any cost.
principles.quote: the final 10% costs more than the first 90%.

sources.title: Shaan Puri on storytelling: intention and obstacle, frames, emotion-first writing, and state
sources.originalTitle: How to Tell an Unforgettable Story (The Shaan Puri Interview)
sources.summary: Shaan shares a practical storytelling and writing system: intention and obstacle, five-second moments of change, and framing over hooks. He covers working backwards from a target emotion, changing your state before you write, editing by removing the suck, and building a binge bank so audience trust compounds over time.

principles.text: Every story needs a clear intention and an obstacle; if viewers can't say what the hero wants and what blocks them, attention drifts.
principles.quote: you should be able to pause at any moment and just point at the screen and just say, "What's What do they want right now? And what's in their way?"

principles.text: A story is a five-second moment of change; stakes come from the emotion on the line, not from life-or-death drama.
principles.quote: A story is a five-second moment of change.

principles.text: Frames beat hooks: reframing an idea and connecting unrelated ideas matters more than a clickbait first line.
principles.quote: Hooks are about the words you're going to write. Frames are about the idea and how you're going to make that idea relevant

principles.text: Work backwards from the emotion you want to trigger, since people only share content that makes them react.
principles.quote: the only things people will share is things that are LOL, WTF, OMG, AW

principles.text: Change your state before creating: physiology first, then focus, then the story you tell yourself. Few do this, which makes it an arbitrage.
principles.quote: if you want to basically change your state, physiology first, focus second, story third.

principles.text: Build a binge bank: a library of content that makes someone who goes down the rabbit hole in an hour or two like and respect you.
principles.quote: I need to create this library that if anybody, like if David is going to do research he's going to spend an hour or two hours going like down the rabbit hole

sources.title: Level up your life: strategically broke, project selection, networks and the enjoyment flywheel
sources.originalTitle: Level Up Your Life In 2026 | Shaan Puri
sources.summary: Shaan, interviewed by his former intern, shares philosophies from before he made money: optimize for freedom and learning over cash, move close to what you want, pick projects and partners over grinding, and only do work that is its own reward. Packed with stories (sushi startup, Mr. Beast's 100 videos, selling Bebo).

principles.text: When young and cash-poor, calculate the minimum money needed and optimize for freedom, learning and adventure instead of stacking dollars.
principles.quote: the better thing to do is optimize for freedom, optimize for learning, optimize for adventure and fun um and just calculate the minimum amount of money you need to be able to do that.

principles.text: Proximity is power: get near people already doing the thing you want; pull beats push.
principles.quote: just get around other people who already are doing the thing you want or have the thing you want or also chasing the thing you want.

principles.text: Most people aren't serious, so being serious puts you in a small final pool. Do 100 reps, improving one thing each time.
principles.quote: You're going to make 100 videos... pick one thing you're going to do better.

principles.text: Ask whether you'd start this project today if you weren't already in it; inertia keeps people in mediocre work.
principles.quote: is this business opportunity idea so good that you would tomorrow pick up the phone, call these same people you're working with and say, let's do this same thing.

principles.text: Only do work that is its own reward; enjoyment creates a flywheel of practice, skill and results.
principles.quote: Because you enjoy it, you do it all the time. Because you do it all the time, you get really good at it. Because you get really good at it, you do get the results.

principles.text: Hard work is overrated; project selection and who you work with matter far more, and skills outlast failed projects.
principles.quote: Choosing what you what you work on is far more important than how hard you work.

sources.title: Shaan Puri's contrarian rules: hard work is overrated, enthusiasm and storytelling are underrated
sources.originalTitle: 7 Semi-Controversial Rules For Success - Shaan Puri
sources.summary: Shaan Puri argues project selection and who you work with matter far more than hard work. He calls enthusiasm and storytelling underrated skills, says to change your state by acting rather than thinking, and warns most people learn the wrong lesson from failure.

principles.text: What you work on and who you work with matter far more than how hard you work.
principles.quote: hard work will let you win the game that you're playing but it doesn't help you if you chose the wrong game and so the most critical decision is actually project selection

principles.text: Enthusiasm is a skill: borrow future excitement today, since belief drives action, which drives results.
principles.quote: enthusiasm is borrowing from the future and um I think it's a skill I think it is massively underrated

principles.text: Good stories rest on intention and obstacle, then stakes; few people learn this, so a little effort puts you ahead.
principles.quote: stories are about intention and obstacle

principles.text: To change how you feel, change what you do; thinking your way out usually ties you in knots.
principles.quote: if you do a thing you will feel differently which will cause you to think differently

principles.text: Most people don't learn from failure; keep a written system to assess your decisions later.
principles.quote: people should have a system to assess the decisions you make because judgment and decision making is probably the most important skill you can hone over time

principles.text: Use a few principles and apply them; wisdom is doing, not collecting more knowledge.
principles.quote: knowledge is knowing what you should do and wisdom is doing what you should do

sources.title: How Shaan Puri and Ben Levy engineer luck, relationships and 9 $1M projects
sources.summary: Shaan and his business partner Ben Levy explain how they pick a new mission every 3-6 months, treat luck as a metric you track, and build relationships through lightweight texts plus long in-person hangs. They also riff on half-baked ideas like rebranding ugly categories and paid hardship experiences.

principles.text: Give people irrational early belief and tell them out loud; a first believer is a starting ingredient before cash.
principles.quote: everybody I know who's successful in life at some point had somebody who irrationally believed in them

principles.text: Treat luck as a skill: track the lucky breaks and the activities that create them, then do more of them.
principles.quote: we took luck and we actually made it like a business metric that you measure.

principles.text: What gets measured gets managed: log daily luck-creating actions and trace which ones later paid off.
principles.quote: the Peter Ducker mantra, what gets measured gets managed. Let's actually treat luck like something you can actually manage.

principles.text: Relationship barbell: stay lightweight over text or go deep in person for hours; avoid the middle-zone call.
principles.quote: It's death by a thousand Zoom calls. So like a 40-minute Zoom call or 45minut Zoom call is basically the worst of both worlds.

principles.text: Content attracts the right people; a dedicated extroverted partner then meets, helps and connects them on your behalf.
principles.quote: Gary is like building a magnet to attract people who like what he's all about, right? That's his content that he's putting out there.

principles.text: Gather a curated peer group of owners at your level so every problem you hit is already solved by someone in the room.
principles.quote: whatever problem we had somebody in that group had already had that problem and could answer it and so it just accelerated our business learning so fast

sources.title: Shaan Puri on audience-first businesses: the trust equation, sticky growth, and when to quit
sources.originalTitle: Shaan Puri’s 3 Step Formula For Finding Your 1000 True Fans (#142)
sources.summary: Shaan shares how he learned audience-building from Bebo and Steven Bartlett's theme-page "Thunder Clap", why podcasts are the hardest audience to grow, and his "trust equation" for valuing audiences. He also covers how to choose projects, stay patient with results, and decide when to quit.

principles.text: Value an audience by quality x size x trust, not by follower count alone.
principles.quote: the trust equation is basically the following three variables. It's the quality of the audience times the size, the number of those people, times the amount that, that they trust me.

principles.text: Hunt for underpriced attention: channels with more trust than their headline numbers suggest, like Twitch streamers.
principles.quote: as a marketer you need to be like looking for which assets are like underpriced 'cause they have more trust than their headline number.

principles.text: Promote in a way that doesn't feel like promotion: no links, no hard sell, create curiosity instead.
principles.quote: there's something to the like fake authenticity of like you're talking about it 'cause you're paid to do it essentially. But you talk about it in a way that brings people in and makes them curious and doesn't just push a product at them.

principles.text: Podcasts lack viral and paid engines, so they only grow through a sticky experience that people voluntarily recommend, slowly.
principles.quote: the sticky engine of growth is basically when somebody uses you, they really use you. They just stick with it. Their engagement deepens the more they do it.

principles.text: Only go audience-first if you'd create the content even if it never grows; it's not an easier path to a business.
principles.quote: you should enjoy the content creation stuff so much that you would be willing to do it even if it didn't work out. That's kind of like, those are the people that survive.

principles.text: Be impatient with action and patient with results; greatness takes longer than beginners expect.
principles.quote: Impatience with action, patience with results.

sources.title: Shaan Puri's 3-step plan to figure out what you want: pop the bubble, wander, look for clues
sources.originalTitle: the 3-step plan to figuring out what you want
sources.summary: Shaan explains how to find a career you'll stick with through the "decade of suck": test-drive jobs before committing, take a time-boxed season of wandering, and hunt for clues (energy and blueprints). Love is framed as a competitive advantage because people who love it practice more.

principles.text: Test-drive your dream job for two weeks before committing; shadowing exposes false dreams cheaply.
principles.quote: Instead of just talking about it - take it for a 2 week test drive. **Try before you buy.**

principles.text: Those who survive the long flat stretch play to play, not to win; enjoying the game keeps you going.
principles.quote: The people that make it through the ‘decade of suck’ are the ones who enjoy the game. They don’t play to win, they play to play.

principles.text: Name and time-box a 'season of wandering' (3 to 12 months) to explore without prematurely committing.
principles.quote: **Give yourself a “Season of Wandering”** - take 3 to 12 months where you experiment & follow your curiosity. Test drive before you buy.

principles.text: Look for clues, not answers: find what feels like play to you but looks like work to others.
principles.quote: But the real clue is to figure out: **what feels like play to you, but looks like work to others?** That’s the moneymaker.

principles.text: Find blueprints: study people already living the life you want, and get specific about what you want.
principles.quote: The fastest shortcut in self improvement is to find someone who _already has what he wants_ and download the blueprint of their habits & mindset.

principles.text: Get outside your bubble and be near the people doing what you want; proximity reveals far more ways to win.
principles.quote: **Turns out there are 10,000x more “ways to win” than you even realized existed.**

sources.title: How Shaan Puri spent a year "strategically broke" and learned master skills through projects
sources.originalTitle: how i spent a year 'strategically broke' (and why it was the best decision of my life)
sources.summary: Shaan explains how he funded a no-job year in his 20s by calculating the minimum money needed for maximum freedom, living cheap, and earning via tutoring, coaching and business plan competition prizes. He then used the time to build "master skills" through low-stakes projects that each sucked a little less.

principles.text: Calculate the minimum money you need for maximum freedom instead of trying to maximize income.
principles.quote: Instead of trying to figure out how to make the most money, we calculated the minimum money needed to live with max freedom.

principles.text: When you hit a time cap, ask for a one-time move that delivers your whole goal; constraints breed creativity.
principles.quote: constraints breed creativity. I asked myself “what’s something easy I could do once, that would give me my entire year goal?”

principles.text: You can get paid for pitching an idea without building the business, e.g. niche business plan competitions with low competition.
principles.quote: I could just pitch the idea, and get paid for the pitch (without even doing the business).

principles.text: Trade nice stuff for freedom of time when young; early years compound in skills and relationships.
principles.quote: A year of free time in your 20s is worth a decade of free time when you retire at 65.

principles.text: Learn master skills that unlock many doors, like hustle, selling online and persuasion.
principles.quote: That’s a master skill. A skill that unlocks many doors in the future.

principles.text: Ship rough version 1.0 projects and iterate; every first version sucks, so keep removing the suck.
principles.quote: Every version 1.0 of everything, sucks.  So your job is to edit, and tweak, over and over again until… it no longer sucks.

sources.title: Creativity loves constraints: Dr. Seuss, Jaws, and the One Minute Blog
sources.summary: Shaan argues that tight constraints unleash creativity rather than limit it. He uses Dr. Seuss's 50-word bet and Spielberg's broken shark in Jaws as examples, then points to his own 'One Minute Blog' format as a self-imposed constraint that outperforms his no-limit posts.

principles.text: Constraints unleash creativity, just as self-discipline unlocks personal freedom.
principles.quote: Similarly - Constraints are what unleash creativity.

principles.text: When a constraint is forced on you, embrace it instead of fighting it; it can produce a better result.
principles.quote: They were about to pause production, when Speilberg had an idea: Embrace the constraint.

principles.text: Impose artificial constraints on yourself, like a hard length cap, to force sharper work.
principles.quote: I call this series the “One Minute Blog” - as a constraint. Can I write something insightful that only takes the reader 1min 59sec max to read?

principles.text: Constrained formats can outperform unconstrained ones; his short posts beat his no-limit posts.
principles.quote: My “One Minute” posts are _far more_ popular than my no-limit posts.

principles.text: Great creators work inside a tight box rather than thinking outside it.
principles.quote: “Think outside the box” was wrong. What great creators do is put themselves _into_ a tight box to do their best work.

principles.text: Cutting resources, like budget, can spark creativity.
principles.quote: "Creativity starts when you cut a zero from your budget." — Jaime Lerner

sources.title: Finding your thing: ask what everyone else is mysteriously bad at
sources.summary: Shaan argues that finding your 'thing' is the only true shortcut in life. Instead of asking what you're great at, notice what everyone else seems mysteriously bad at. He found explaining things after 10 years of being a B+ founder, and his cofounder Ben Levy built a business advantage from staying in touch.

principles.text: Finding your thing is the only true shortcut in life; everyone you admire found theirs.
principles.quote: Finding your thing is the only true shortcut to life.

principles.text: Don't ask what you're great at. Ask what everyone else is mysteriously bad at.
principles.quote: instead of asking “what am I great at?” – just start to pay attention to “what does everyone else mysteriously suck at?”

principles.text: Wanting a skill to be your thing doesn't make it so; being B+ at something won't get you far in the real world.
principles.quote: I was a B+ at it. But in the real world, B+ doesn’t get you jack sh*t.

principles.text: Shaan's thing was explaining things clearly, which he found by doing it for fun (podcast, writing), and it took off.
principles.quote: Then I started podcasting for fun. I started writing. I started doing the thing I thought others were mysteriously bad at (explaining things).

principles.text: Consistently staying in touch is a rare strength that compounds into opportunities and real money.
principles.quote: We’ve directly made millions of dollars just because Ben happened to be staying in touch with someone and they thought of us when an opportunity sprang up.

principles.text: People are often too humble or self-critical to admit what they're great at, so look for the thing others find hard that you find easy.
principles.quote: most of us are too humble, or worse too self-critical to even admit what we’re great at.

sources.title: Underdo the competition: counter-position by being simpler, not better
sources.summary: Shaan argues that instead of out-featuring rivals, you can win by deliberately doing less. Using Slate's $25k stripped-down electric truck and Nintendo's low-fi Wii as examples, he shows how counter-positioning turns last place in a crowded market into first place in a new one.

principles.text: Underdo the competition: go simpler and cheaper when everyone else keeps adding complexity.
principles.quote: They used one of my favorite business tactics: **underdoing the competition.**

principles.text: All positioning is counter-positioning: define yourself by being the opposite of the category norm.
principles.quote: In marketing: all positioning is counter-positioning.

principles.text: Subtract features (screens, heated seats, range) to create a clear, simple product identity at a low price.
principles.quote: Slate went the opposite direction:

principles.text: Reframe the category so you win first place in a niche instead of last place in the mainstream market.
principles.quote: Instead of being **last place** in the fancy electric car market, they’re now **first place** in the simple, fun electric truck market.

principles.text: Don't aim to be the best, aim to be the only.
principles.quote: As Kevin Kelly says: _“Don’t aim to be the best, be the only”._

principles.text: Nintendo's Wii won by being cheaper and simpler than rivals chasing cutting-edge graphics, selling over 100M units.
principles.quote: It sold over 100M+ units, outselling both Xbox & Playstation at the time.

sources.title: Big Mario marketing: sell the customer's transformation, not your product
sources.summary: Shaan's first rule of marketing: nobody cares about your product, they care about themselves. Use the Mario analogy (customer is little Mario, product is the power-up, result is big Mario) and market the outcome the customer gets, not the features.

principles.text: Nobody cares about your product; they care about themselves. This is Rule #1 of marketing.
principles.quote: **Rule #1 of marketing:** “nobody cares about your product, they care about themselves.”

principles.text: Frame the customer as little Mario, your product as the power-up, and the result as big Mario.
principles.quote: **Your customer** = little Mario, not powerful, needs help

principles.text: Don't talk endlessly about yourself; tell customers how awesome they'll be after using the product.
principles.quote: tell customers how awesome they will be after using your product.

principles.text: Sell the concrete life outcome, not the ingredient or feature (e.g. time saved and weight lost, not granola).
principles.quote: If you're selling breakfast bars, don't tell me about the granola. Tell me how this bar can save me 20 minutes of time in the mornings

principles.text: Your product is an obstacle to the customer: it costs money, takes time to learn, and is a necessary evil toward what they really want.
principles.quote: In fact, your product is an obstacle. It has a cost, it takes time to learn, it is a necessary evil on the way to them getting what they _really want_.

principles.text: Everyone cares about improving their own quality of life; marketing starts with understanding this.
principles.quote: But everybody cares about their own quality of life improving.

sources.title: The K-shaped economy: treat your job as a bundle of tasks and learn to manage AI
sources.summary: Shaan argues the AI future is K-shaped: people either get replaced or become 10X more productive by using AI. His fix is to break your job into a bundle of tasks, see which AI can already boost, and learn to manage robots.

principles.text: The AI future is K-shaped: get replaced by AI, or learn to use it and become far more productive.
principles.quote: You have a choice. Either get replaced by AI, or learn to use it and become 10X more productive.

principles.text: Stop seeing your job as one big thing. See it as a bundle of tasks and audit each one for AI leverage.
principles.quote: Stop thinking of your job as 1 big thing. Instead - think of your job as a "bundle of tasks".

principles.text: Today AI only boosts a few of your tasks, but it improves fast, so expect half to be automated soon.
principles.quote: But AI is improving fast. Soon, half your tasks will be handled by AI.

principles.text: Managing AI agents will become more valuable than managing people, so learn the tools now.
principles.quote: in the future being able to "manage robots" will be more valuable than managing humans.

sources.title: Triangle of Talent: Hire Problem Solvers Who Pick the Right Problem
sources.summary: Shaan argues that a few star employees create most of a company's value, yet managers spend most of their time on problem and average employees. He defines stars as people who identify the right problem and then solve it, alone or by coordinating others. He also gives target percentages of "level 5" players by company size.

principles.text: A minority of star employees create about 90% of company value, but managers spend 90% of time on problem and average employees.
principles.quote: But it’s the people on the right side (the star employees) that create 90% of the value in the company.

principles.text: Ignore job titles: every employee is a problem solver, and problem solving has two parts, picking the problem and solving it.
principles.quote: Forget job titles:** All employees are problem solvers

principles.text: Stars identify the right problem and then solve it, either themselves or by coordinating others.
principles.quote: Are you able to solve that problem – either alone, or by coordinating other people?

principles.text: Choosing which problem to solve is easier and more impactful than solving it; ask daily, weekly, monthly and annually what the A+ problem is.
principles.quote: most people think the job is about solving the problem, and it kinda is, but the easier and more impactful thing is getting good at figuring out "what problem needs to be solved right now?"

principles.text: Your team is your company, so build a great team with as many top performers as possible.
principles.quote: the team you build is the company you build… so build a great team.

principles.text: Target share of level 5 stars shrinks with size: 100% for cofounders, 30%+ at 5-20 people, 15% at 20-150, 5-10% at 150+.
principles.quote: If you're a small team (5-20 people) - you should have at least 30%

sources.title: How Shaan Puri would build an audience from scratch: 9 non-obvious lessons
sources.originalTitle: i got internet famous... if i started again from scratch, here's what I'd do this time
sources.summary: Shaan, who has built 500k+ email subscribers, 400k+ Twitter followers, 500k+ YouTube subscribers and 100M+ podcast downloads, shares nine lessons for building an audience. Core ideas: optimize for who follows you, not how many; make content about your inner nerd; build a magnet and a "binge bank"; sell a feeling; and get good through reps.

principles.text: Optimize for who follows you, not how many. One high-quality follower can outweigh thousands of low-quality ones.
principles.quote: Ferrari has 200x LESS customers than GM, yet is still more valuable.

principles.text: Make content about your inner nerd. It eliminates competition and makes every day of making it a win.
principles.quote: I shift the odds of success from 1% to 100% because I win by playing (vs. only winning by winning).

principles.text: Treat content as a magnet that attracts the people you want in your life, not just an audience.
principles.quote: The internet makes it easy to find the 10,000 people who share my flavor of weird.

principles.text: Share the 5Ds (Done, Deliver, Do, Dreams, Dork Out) so people know you well and send you relevant links, books and deals.
principles.quote: I don’t want to be well known. I want to be _known well_.

principles.text: Content substance beats packaging early on. Spend time living an interesting life, not polishing delivery.
principles.quote: A+ content with C- delivery is a great starting point.

principles.text: Build a binge bank: about an hour of your best content that makes a newcomer love you, so small early numbers still compound.
principles.quote: A binge bank is like a personal Netflix binge-worthy show. It’s 1 hour worth of content, that if someone consumed, they would love me.

sources.title: Why "life balance" fails: integrate your life instead of rationing it
sources.originalTitle: why the 'safe path' is not actually safe
sources.summary: Shaan argues balance is the wrong goal because it turns life into a zero-sum rationing game. His alternative is integration: stack goals into single activities and pick work that pays for results, feels like play, and leaves you control of your schedule.

principles.text: Don't ration effort across life areas; integrate them so one hour fills several buckets.
principles.quote: Integration multiplies your time. We all have ~16 waking hours a day, but when you use 1 hour to fill up 3 life buckets – you've multiplied your time.

principles.text: Balance means giving every area 50% effort, a recipe for mediocrity; it is a zero-sum trap.
principles.quote: You'll end up giving every area of your life 50% effort, so that nothing goes to 0% and nothing gets to 100%. A recipe for mediocrity & disappointment.

principles.text: Pick a career paid for results, not time in chair, so you earn well and own your hours.
principles.quote: you build a career where you get paid for results (rather than your hourly time), so you can make a ton of money, and have the freedom of time to spend with family.

principles.text: Use the time test to check whether a job truly rewards results.
principles.quote: if you came to work for an hour, then closed your laptop and left, having done as much work as your co-worker who sits there for 8 hours - Would your boss be mad at you or your coworker?

principles.text: Find work you'd do as a hobby, with results-based pay, 10-100x upside for the best, and schedule control.
principles.quote: where the best people get paid 10x or 100x more than the avg (this is almost everything.

principles.text: Look for 'cheat code' careers and commit, turning down safer offers that pull you away.
principles.quote: now that I knew 'cheat codes' to career existed, I was going to go for that. I said no to every job offer or term sheet to start a new company.

sources.title: Shaan Puri on why "down" is the one trait to look for in a business or life partner
sources.summary: Shaan argues the single most important trait in a partner is being "down": quick to commit, willing to do whatever the mission needs, and biased toward immediate action. He illustrates with his partner Ben, Greg Brockman at OpenAI, Airbnb and Uber, and explains why down partners enable pivots and high-upside bets.

principles.text: The most important trait in a partner, business or life, is being "down": flexible, mission-first, and quick to act.
principles.quote: When picking a partner, the most important thing is to find someone who is **“down”.**

principles.text: Being down is an action word, not a personality trait; down people start now and figure things out along the way.
principles.quote: Down isn’t just a personality trait (like, ‘smart’). Down is an action word. People who are down take action now. They don’t wait. They don’t overthink. They just start, and figure things out.

principles.text: Fast committers get far more shots on goal, which outweighs the occasional miss from under-thinking.
principles.quote: Even if they miss something 1 out of 10 times, they move 10x faster than over-thinkers, and so they get 10 times more shots on goal.

principles.text: A partner who flinches at uncertainty silently filters out high-upside ideas before you even raise them.
principles.quote: When your partner isn’t down, you pre-filter all the high upside paths out before they even see the light of day.

principles.text: Most great businesses pivot, and a mid-air U-turn only works if your partner is down.
principles.quote: You can only pull off that type of mid-air U-Turn if your partner is _down_. Weak stomachs can’t handle the sudden shifts.

principles.text: Great partners are not necessarily the smartest or hardest working; Ben was neither but was chosen for being down.
principles.quote: If Ben is one thing - Ben is down. No matter what comes up, he’s down for the cause, down to try it, down to start, right now.

sources.title: The Elon Method: how Elon Musk went all in to swing the election
sources.summary: Shaan retells 22 events that pushed Elon into backing Trump and extracts his operating pattern: find the existential problem, pick the key lever, burn the boats. Also covers risk as game theory, +EV bets with outsized upside, and separating credibility from likeability.

principles.text: Attack the biggest existential problem, find the key lever, then commit everything to it.
principles.quote: 1. Figure out what is the most Existential Problem 2. Identify the key lever (eg. PA swing state) 3. Go all in. Burn all boats. Throw your entire weight at it

sources.title: Excuses: you always pick a reason, so pick one that moves you forward
sources.summary: Shaan argues every reason we give ourselves is really an excuse we choose to believe, and that excuses can push us toward action or away from it. Using a trainer, Hormozi's hero/villain line and Mike Posner's rattlesnake story, he says setbacks can be reasons to quit or to restart.

principles.text: An excuse is just a reason you make up and choose to believe, so it can be positive or negative.
principles.quote: An excuse is simply a reason that you make up and choose to believe in.

principles.text: The same circumstance can fuel action or inaction; the difference is which excuse you pick.
principles.quote: He found an excuse to do it. I found an excuse to not do it.

principles.text: Pain is the common starting point; what matters is whether you use it or it uses you.
principles.quote: Heroes use pain. Villains are used by it.

principles.text: A setback can be an excuse to stop or an excuse to restart; restarting changes who you become.
principles.quote: Either this is an excuse to stop. Or it's an excuse to restart. So I went back and restarted. And when I did that, I became someone new.

principles.text: Realize all reasons are excuses, then deliberately choose ones that make you feel good and do good.
principles.quote: Are you going to find excuses to feel shitty, and be shitty? Or find excuses to feel good, and do good?

sources.title: Mispriced assets: look for what's overlooked, from stocks to showmanship
sources.summary: Shaan uses a Weight Watchers stock call (down 90%+, then up 166% in a month) to introduce "mispriced assets": things that are overlooked or misunderstood. He applies the lens to personality traits, arguing showmanship and playfulness are undervalued, and illustrates it with a basketball-coach prank.

principles.text: Hunt for mispriced assets: things overlooked or misunderstood by the market, not just stocks.
principles.quote: But I tell you this story to bring up the idea of **“mispriced assets”** - things that are overlooked, or misunderstood.

principles.text: When a well-known company's stock collapses on a temporary shock while demand persists, it may be mispriced.
principles.quote: Did weight loss go away? Was it a trend? Nope. We’re still fatter than ever.

principles.text: Apply the mispricing lens to daily life, including which personality traits are undervalued.
principles.quote: Stocks are cool, but I look for mispriced assets in my daily life.

principles.text: Showmanship is an undervalued trait because everyone else is staring at phones; scarcity raises its value.
principles.quote: The more we’ve become bent-neck nerds, staring at phones, old school showmanship has become rare.

principles.text: A small dose of playfulness can create outsized delight and memorability in 10 seconds.
principles.quote: It took 10 seconds, but just choosing to have a little showmanship, or playfulness, made this guys day.

principles.text: Don't let adulthood beat the fun out of you; deliberately find moments for style and play.
principles.quote: Today - find a moment to play. Find a moment to do something with a little finesse.

sources.title: Power brokers: the voice in your head writes your reality, so pick the story that serves you
sources.summary: Shaan argues the most important voice in your life is your inner monologue, which acts as director of your life's movie. Events are neutral; the meaning you attach is a choice, so when the voice spews negativity (like after launching his podcast), ask it for other stories and pick the one that serves you.

principles.text: The most influential voice in your life is your own inner voice, not parents, teachers or friends.
principles.quote: The most important voice in your life is the one that no one else hears. It’s the **voice in your head.**

principles.text: The stories you tell yourself become your reality, so you can reprogram your default self-talk.
principles.quote: The power broker in your life is the voice that no one ever hears. It is the master storyteller, and the stories we tell ourselves are our reality

principles.text: Events are neutral; the meaning you put on them makes them positive or negative.
principles.quote: Everything in your life is neutral. **It’s the meaning we put ON it that gives it a positive or negative spin.**

principles.text: When launching something new, the inner voice can tell opposing stories; the true one is whichever you believe.
principles.quote: Which story is true? **Whichever one you believe.**

principles.text: Pause when your inner voice turns negative, ask for alternative stories, and choose the one that serves you.
principles.quote: Next time you hear the tiny voice in your head - try to pause and ask it to come up with other stories. What else is on the menu? What else could be true? And then pick the story that serves you.

principles.text: Life is made up, but you get to author it (endorsing Garry Tan's framing).
principles.quote: the key to life is realizing that it’s all made up… but you get to make it up

sources.title: Proximity is power: why moving to the right place is the easiest self-improvement lever
sources.summary: Shaan answers a reader stuck in a "good but not great" life with one word: move. He explains how he left a cushy job in Australia for San Francisco, where the surrounding culture reset his ambition, and argues you should relocate to wherever your people are densest.

principles.text: Changing your surroundings is often the easiest form of self-improvement; plant yourself in great soil.
principles.quote: sometimes the easiest thing to do is change your surroundings.

principles.text: Go where the best environment for your goal is, even with no job or contacts there.
principles.quote: I quit my job and moved to Gotham City (aka San Francisco) - where I had no job, and didn’t know anybody.

principles.text: A city where your goal is normal and the alternative is weird makes status work in your favor, a powerful motivator.
principles.quote: I realized that SF is the only city in the world where startups are normal, and jobs are weird. The high-status thing was low-status here. That’s a powerful motivator.

principles.text: Every place has a cultural whisper that shapes your drive; pick the one that pushes you toward your ambition.
principles.quote: The whisper isn’t always healthy, but it’s always motivating.

principles.text: Moving resets your routines, social circle, pace, thinking and lifestyle all at once.
principles.quote: Moving will shake up your social circle. Your pace. Your thinking. Your lifestyle.

principles.text: Move to where the highest density of people nerdy about your thing live; proximity is power.
principles.quote: Whatever the thing you’re nerdy about - where is the highest density of like-minded nerds?

sources.title: Shamelessly cloning: copy what works instead of being the stubborn gas station owner
sources.summary: Shaan retells Mohnish Pabrai's story of building a $100M+ fortune through "shamelessly cloning", using Tom Peters' parable of two gas stations. Most people watch a competitor win and still don't change their behavior, so deliberately becoming a great copier of great ideas is an edge. Copy the idea and add your own twist, not the exact art.

principles.text: Become a great copier of great ideas; most people refuse to copy what they can see working, which is the edge.
principles.quote: Mohnish thought this was ridiculous & made a promise to himself that he would become a **great copier of great ideas.**

principles.text: The interesting question isn't what the smart operator does, but why competitors who see it working don't copy it.
principles.quote: Most people want to study what the smart owner does. But I think the more interesting question is: “why the heck is owner B _not_ doing what he sees is working??”

principles.text: Even if you hand competitors your trade secrets, they usually won't change behavior, so copying is under-exploited.
principles.quote: You can go to your direct competitors, and tell them all your trade secrets. Everything you’ve learned. They will listen to you but there will be **no change in behavior.**

principles.text: Small, compounding service improvements can multiply a commodity business's revenue.
principles.quote: As time goes on, **Owner A** continues to make small improvements to his service. Eventually he’s making 2-3x more per week than the station across the street.

principles.text: Copy the underlying idea, not the exact artifact, and put your own twist on it.
principles.quote: I’d say the gas station owner shouldn’t copy the exact signage, but the idea of “I should make my business look more approachable too” and put his own twist on it.

principles.text: You don't need to be the one who figures everything out; you can simply choose not to be the owner who ignores what works.
principles.quote: You may not be the smart gas station owner who figures everything out. But you _can_ choose to not be the idiot owner across the street.

sources.title: Someday: why the 'safe path' kills your dreams and why now is the only time to start
sources.summary: Shaan argues that "later" and "someday" are the most dangerous words for ambition, because things never settle down and you just stay busy. He urges acting on your dreams now, especially in your 20s "Ramen Era" when you have maximum flexibility and nothing to lose.

principles.text: The 'safe path' isn't safe; it slowly suffocates your ambition and sense of adventure.
principles.quote: The ‘safe path’ is not actually safe. In fact it’s dangerous. It’s dangerous to your dreams.

principles.text: 'Later' never comes. Life doesn't settle down, you just stay busy, so postponing is how dreams die.
principles.quote: But things never settle down. You simply stay busy. And “later” never comes.

principles.text: If you're called to do something, the only right time is now, even at 31 or older.
principles.quote: If you’re called to do something, the only right time is _right now_.

principles.text: Your early 20s are the Ramen Era: maximum flexibility, nothing to lose, so take big risks then.
principles.quote: Sure, you’re broke and have no skills... but you have maximum flexibility and nothing to lose.

principles.text: Staying put trains you like Pavlov's dog and atrophies the muscle to chase what you really want.
principles.quote: But we become pavlovian dogs. Trained to stay put in the stuff we’re doing, and losing the muscle to go chase the stuff we really want.

sources.title: Stop working so hard: find the product that is you pushed out
sources.summary: Shaan argues hard work alone doesn't equal success. The real leverage is finding a business that is a natural extension of who you are, so it feels like play to you and looks like work to others, then becoming the best at it so the internet finds and rewards you.

principles.text: Hard work helps but alone doesn't equal success; pay isn't proportional to sweat.
principles.quote: Hard work helps. Certainly. But hard work alone doesn't equal success.

principles.text: Find the product that is you pushed out: a thing so natural to you it's just being yourself.
principles.quote: Basically - find a thing that's so you, that doing it is just a natural extension of you being yourself.

principles.text: The best work looks like work to others but feels like play to you; that energy attracts demand.
principles.quote: That's the key. Looks like work to others.

principles.text: Turn a fun thing you already do into a business by adding the smallest missing piece, like a microphone.
principles.quote: All we needed to do was add a microphone, and boom. I found the perfect job for me.

principles.text: Become the best at anything and the internet will find you and pay you handsomely.
principles.quote: If you become the best at anything - you get paid handsomely.

principles.text: Pick a career goal: get paid a king's ransom for something you'd do for free.
principles.quote: You can steal my career goal: “Get paid a King's ransom for something that I would do for free.”

sources.title: Who's your Elon?: Pick admired role models and name the price to pay
sources.summary: Shaan argues founders shouldn't default to Elon as their north star; instead pick the career you actually admire. He admires creative polymaths like Ben Franklin and Jesse Itzler, and uses Scott Adams' "find the price and pay it" framing to list the habits that lifestyle demands.

principles.text: Don't blindly copy the most famous founder; ask whose actual life and career you want.
principles.quote: So it begs the question - who do I actually admire? Who’s life/career do I look at and say - ‘gimme one of those’?

principles.text: A role model is a useful guide, not an exact copy.
principles.quote: It’s never an exact copy you want, but a useful guide.

principles.text: Find the price of the success you want, then pay it.
principles.quote: If you want to be successful, find out what the price is and then pay it.

principles.text: Be willing to reinvent yourself and start from scratch with a beginner's mind.
principles.quote: reinvent self and not be afraid to start from scratch (beginner's mind)

principles.text: Become a fast learner and be unafraid of doing things you're clueless at.
principles.quote: be unafraid to do things that I’m clueless at

principles.text: Expect to change career label, friend circle and habits every few years.
principles.quote: be willing to change my career label, friend circle, and habits every few years.

sources.title: Shaan Puri AMA: market crashes, leverage lessons, and reading to spark ideas
sources.originalTitle: AMA: Stock Market Crash, AI Drama, and Naval
sources.summary: Shaan answers reader questions. He shares what getting close to a margin call in the COVID crash taught him about leverage, selling, and doing nothing in a downturn. He also lays out how he reads, after Naval's idea that reading is about sparking thoughts, not collecting information.

principles.text: Treat leverage with caution: too much of it can wreck you in a crash.
principles.quote: Leverage is like botox. Use with caution. Too much of it will f*ck your face up

principles.text: When a market crashes, respond rather than react. Do nothing for 30 days.
principles.quote: When a market crash happens - respond, don’t react. Just _do nothing_ for 30 days

principles.text: Selling early is costlier than buying wrong, because a bad buy caps your loss while an early sale forfeits upside.
principles.quote: The most costly mistakes are about SELLING early (not buying wrong). When you buy wrong, you can only lose 1x your investment max. But selling early, you might miss out on 2-10x upside

principles.text: Read to spark new thoughts, not to collect information.
principles.quote: The point of the books isn’t about getting info, it’s about sparking new thoughts in your mind.

principles.text: Read widely across unrelated subjects so ideas combine in new ways.
principles.quote: Read _a wide range_ of things.** I read a book about management, and then a book called Chimpanzee Politics (_power and sex among apes)_. These unrelated books spark new combinations of ideas in my mind

principles.text: Reread the best books years later, since you are a different person and take away something new.
principles.quote: Rather than read new books, I read books again, several years later. Even though it’s the same book, I’m a different person, so I take something completely different from it.

sources.title: Shaan Puri's mailbag: building a bias for action, "flipping" angel investments, and lessons from Amazon
sources.originalTitle: Bias for action, contrarian investing strategies, and Bezos
sources.summary: Shaan answers reader questions on how to train a bias for action (treat it as a skill, get reps, notice wins, and change the questions you ask yourself). He also pitches an untried angel strategy of flipping seed investments at the next round, shares what he took from Twitch/Amazon (big companies are mediocre inside, writing memos matter), and gives his own definition of AGI.

principles.text: Bias for action is a learnable skill, not a trait; believe that first.
principles.quote: First, you have to believe it’s a skill.** If you don’t believe it’s a skill, then it’s just a trait you’re born with (or without).

principles.text: Build action reps in small, safe areas first so quitting your job isn't your first bold move.
principles.quote: You don’t want “quit my job to start the company” to be the first bold action you’ve ever done. Start by doing it around the house.

principles.text: Notice and reinforce each time you act instead of procrastinating, so your brain collects evidence you are an action-taker.
principles.quote: But doing it isn’t enough. You have to take notice, to reinforce your brain

principles.text: Change the prompt you give your brain: ask how to take massive action and move with speed, not 'will this work?'
principles.quote: Instead of trying to make the AI smarter - it’s much easier to try just changing the prompt first.

principles.text: Early-stage investing has an untried edge: flip seed investments at the next round; the barrier is perception, not rules.
principles.quote: The reason people don’t do it is perception. As an angel investor you’re supposed to be a true believer. You’re supposed to hold till exit/IPO. But those are just cultural norms, not rules.

principles.text: Big tech is less sophisticated inside than startups assume, but its writing culture (clear memos) is worth copying.
principles.quote: The best habit I took away was their writing culture. Writing memos forces a clarity of thought - and is the best way to communicate inside companies.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan covers selling to human nature without being manipulative, simplifying goals into A (where you are), B (next step), Z (the outcome), and why most advice-seeking is really permission-seeking. He argues location, obsession and playfulness matter more than grind, and that success should be balanced rather than extreme.

chunks.heading: The economy runs on fear: sell to the root insecurity, but aim at option three
chunks.text:
- Shaan's observation: "The economy is just smart people paying beautiful people to promote stuff to insecure people."
- Selling by audience:
  - Mothers: sell safety for their children.
  - Women: sell beauty or youth.
  - Men: sell status, power and importance.
- From his club-promoter days: people pay $500 for a bottle that costs $50 across the street, because the club is selling status.
- Know the root insecurity of the buyer and pull the strongest lever.
- The world is predatory by default. He argues you should see it "as it is" before using agency to shift it toward how it should be.
- He cites direct-mail copywriter Gary Halbert: "Never has more money been lost than selling somebody what they should want versus what they do want."
- Meet people where they are. Frame the offer and benefits so they resonate with what people actually want.
- Option one is manipulation that succeeds. Option two is the noble nonprofit that never learned what people want and gets nowhere. Shaan says don't debate them. Two bad options means "go create another one".
- Option three:
  - Combine an understanding of human psychology with a noble cause.
  - Tell stories, and show the happy ending instead of the work required.
  - Sell benefits, not features.
- If you are noble but can't reach people, or can reach people but do nothing noble, you are "pissing your talents away".

chunks.heading: The ABC method: only know A, B and Z
chunks.text:
- Overthinking is highly transmissible. The cure is to simplify.
- The trap is mapping A through Z. Doubt about each step multiplies, and by halfway you are exhausted and paralyzed.
- Only three letters matter:
  - **A:** an honest view of where you are now. Self-delusion stalls you.
  - **B:** the next incremental action toward Z.
  - **Z:** the happy ending you want. It stays fixed.
- Once B is done you have a new A and a new B, and Z stays the same.
- His trainer's corner-store analogy:
  - Walking to the corner store for ice cream, you don't doubt you'll arrive, so you only think about the next turn.
  - He uses this for goals like podcasting, getting in shape or running the race with friends.
  - The trainer notices that high achievers are "stressor achievers": long stress, brief relief, new goalpost, new stress.
- Podcast example:
  - Define Z (his dream guests, his own studio), then describe A honestly: current guests, skill level, outreach volume, prep time.
  - B examples: send ten outreach messages this week, or study how Chris Williamson writes intros (he reads a tweet instead of a long-winded opener).
- Progress equals happiness for Shaan. Humans are wired to feel happy during progress, relative to where they are, so this formula helps you feel good while hitting goals.
- Early-stage projects feel great because of nonlinear momentum: big acceleration from a cold start.

chunks.heading: Advice-seeking is permission-seeking; the world is gated by courage, not intelligence
chunks.text:
- "All requests for advice are actually requests for permission." People "don't want information. They want a short-term loan on courage."
- Asking five people for advice is usually looking for someone to validate the decision you already want to make, like wanting someone to approve your parking.
- His tweet: the world is not intelligence-gated. The real gates are courage, action, energy and wisdom. Plenty of people no smarter than us have better marriages and lives.
- Ask yourself "what permission am I seeking?" Often you already know which direction you're called to go, and fear is why you aren't going.
- Giving it to yourself:
  - Support from others is nice. He asks successful people "who was your first believer?" and they can answer immediately.
  - You can also grant the permission yourself once you see that's what you want.
- Example: his piano and singing teacher got him to try singing, and said he had worked with people who started worse. The teacher had not sung until high school, was mocked for it and shut it down, until a choir teacher heard him and said "who told you you can't sing?" He said not singing "was killing me."
- Fear underlies every label:
  - Procrastination, stress and anxiety are "fancy words" for fear.
  - Ask "why" about fear of failure and it ends at "I'm not enough, I won't be loved."
- Courage is feeling fear and acting anyway. Nobody calls a sip of water brave, unless the person drinking has a private terror of it.
- Parenting example:
  - His son wouldn't go into classes (jiu-jitsu, tennis, basketball). Shaan stopped getting frustrated and told him he used to cry at gymnastics too.
  - He framed it as courage and fear fighting, "Pikachu vs. Charizard", where sometimes fear wins. A month later his son said, "I didn't want to let the fear win today."

chunks.heading: Move to the white-hot center of your interest; soil matters more than the flower
chunks.text:
- His claim: moving to San Francisco was the most impactful thing he did.
- The founder-market line: "when a great founder meets a bad market, only one of them retains their reputation. It's the bad market." The same applies to life: "It is far easier to succeed in great soil."
- Inertia and attachment to the familiar (hometown, friends, job) keep people in soil they wouldn't choose if they started from scratch.
- His advice to anyone in their 20s: move to the white-hot center of your interest.
  - Proximity is power. Ideally live in the same house as people with similar dreams.
  - He calls it "the single greatest variable you can change in your life", more than any book or podcast.
- What San Francisco taught him on day one:
  - At a coffee shop he overheard a founder pitching "peptides for dogs" to an investor.
  - That night a JP Morgan employee at a startup event apologized for his job and said he'd leave soon. Status there goes to chasing a startup idea, not to working at big corp.
  - Before that, he had been the weird one for being unemployed and trying to build something.
- Seasons: what is right in one season of life may not be in another. Answer the call you feel, and moving can accelerate it.

chunks.heading: Follow obsession, use fuel sources deliberately, and connect the dots by making them bold
chunks.text:
- Discipline, motivation and obsession:
  - Shaan treats them as different fuel sources for the same engine: discipline (Goggins), inspiration or motivation, and obsession.
  - He compares them to calories. Some are clean and sustainable, some are dirty and unsustainable, and you choose which fuel you use.
- "Inspiration is like an avocado": very perishable, so act on it quickly.
- Trusting yourself to follow inspiration even when you don't know where it leads is a muscle and a way of living, "like some people sit upright, some people slouch."
- Steve Jobs example:
  - Jobs took a calligraphy class in college out of pure interest.
  - That led the Mac to launch with multiple fonts, which helped it succeed.
  - You can't connect dots looking forward, so "make every dot as bold as you can": do genuine-interest things fully, without knowing where they lead.
- Windows vs. doors:
  - A friend (his mentor) told the youngest VC in San Francisco, "you only want to open windows, never doors." Windows let you see the other side first. With a door you knock without knowing.
  - Sometimes nobody answers or the other side isn't what you wanted, but knocking enough times creates surface area for luck.
  - Shaan now asks where he is gravitating toward windows and which door he could knock on.

chunks.heading: Winning is balanced success; the final 10% costs more than the first 90%
chunks.text:
- After selling a company he had "all the money I'll ever need", then hit the "dog who caught the car" problem: who am I if not the person chasing this?
- He hired a coach, Dr. Jack Kane (met through Andrew Wilkinson), who told him the fable of Iron John.
  - The three types of men in the story: good boys, wild men and great kings.
  - A good boy pleases others and does what is expected: school, job, house, two kids, country club. He has dissatisfaction because he never asked what his soul wanted.
  - A wild man is a free man, not a bad man. He is courageous, disciplined, has principles and serves his own needs.
  - A great king is a wild man who starts caring about things beyond himself, and "a good boy never becomes a great king."
  - Shaan says he's the wild man today and wants to become the great king.
- His circle-of-care model:
  - A baby cares only about itself. Each new thing you care about forces you to grow.
  - When you care about something more than your comfort, you have to change.
  - A king serves a kingdom (family, friends, community, strangers online, people with a rare disease).
- The "what serves you most will also screw you" idea:
  - His own superpower, storytelling and persuasion, means he is "patient zero" for his own persuasion.
  - He uses a sword/power-tool analogy: know the downside and wield it with care.
- "Arrival fallacy":
  - Many people who hit their goals become aimless, or run it back to prove it wasn't luck (he cites an Airbnb founder).
  - He is less impressed by success than by success achieved with balance, fun and being a good person.
  - His view: pure success has a formula, while success plus a good marriage, family and integrated self is "much closer to art than science."
- "Greatness bubble":
  - Nonlinear progress means beginner's gains come fast, then a plateau, then the last 10% costs enormously.
  - Extremes (bodybuilders, billionaires, Olympians) are highly visible but not desirable.
  - Shaan: "We confuse an extraordinary result with an extraordinary life." He knows "bankrupt billionaires" and "fat doctors."
  - He admires Goggins for one hour a day (workouts) and doesn't want to be him.
- Kevin Kelly story: asked what being Kevin Kelly cost, he said the cost was "greatness". He surrendered the biggest-empire version for a freer life.
- "Enough" is the revolutionary stance: it's okay to be satisfied.
- Be great, don't just accomplish great things:
  - Be great in moment-to-moment interactions, like how you greet someone or compliment a shirt.
  - Example: a friend, Ramon, a single dad, started a football team for his son and later coached other boys with no football background. He was asked to give the commencement speech, and instead brought a formerly shy kid on stage and played "Gangnam Style".

chunks.heading: Relationships: heal to 101%, ask "what are we trying to do here?", and reset with play
chunks.text:
- Gottman insight: he claims Gottman could predict with about 90% accuracy whether couples stay together from watching them briefly. It's about how well you fight, not compatibility.
- After every cut, relationships heal to either 99% or 101%. Heal to 99% and the relationship degrades over time. A small 2% swing matters.
- In the moment you're focused on the cut ("how dare you"), not the healing.
- Ask "what are we trying to do here?" Not about the situation: "I love you. You love me. We're on the same team."
- Reaction vs. response:
  - Great people respond instead of reacting. We give better advice to others than to ourselves because in conflict we go into fight-or-flight.
  - Rewind phrase: "I didn't like my reaction back there, let me try again." He literally makes a rewind sound effect at home.
- Improv lesson:
  - The first class taught nothing about being funny. It was about failing: when you say something stupid, say "whoop," and everyone responds "whoop," like shaking an Etch A Sketch.
  - Lesson: have a way to clear the slate.
- Play can break tension when logic can't.
  - He tells a story (admitting he doesn't know how true it is) of a US president who walked out of a tense Russia meeting, turned at the door and playfully reintroduced himself.
  - Humor, silliness and play are legitimate tools alongside "heavy" emotional work.
  - "We're not as sophisticated as we hope to believe" (a laugh track makes things funnier).
- His current focus: making a movie, building a "crazy magic thing" in New York, and "projects with the boys", picking creative projects with inspiring people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan shares a practical storytelling and writing system: intention and obstacle, five-second moments of change, and framing over hooks. He covers working backwards from a target emotion, changing your state before you write, editing by removing the suck, and building a binge bank so audience trust compounds over time.

chunks.heading: Frame the idea, not just the hook
chunks.text:
- Shaan says hooks are "somewhat overrated" and frames are underrated. A hook is the attention-grabbing first line. A frame is how you present the idea itself, and how you make it relevant by connecting two ideas that seem unrelated.
- Example: instead of describing what Hasan Minhaj does to open a set, frame it as "Here's what you can learn about public speaking from one of the greatest public speakers in the world." Same content, new frame.
- He argues the great writers are great at framing ideas, more than at writing the perfect one-line hook.
- His Clubhouse thread used a frame: "everyone seems to think Clubhouse is the next big thing, but I think it's going to fail. Here's how I think it all goes down." The thread (about 20 million readers) was written like a screenplay: "you're the founder of Clubhouse," with a setup of Kanye in your DMs and VCs throwing money at you.
- The contrast was a dry thread by the founder of Secret that opened with jargon ("existential threat number one, time to value ratio"). Shaan says it felt like homework.
- He says "here's how it goes down" is gossip and story, while "here's why I'm right" is logic.
- His Dave Chappelle example: Chappelle wanted people to boycott Netflix over his show. He told two stories (a veteran comedian taking his joke when he was 15, and losing $100 to a three-card monte crew) and framed Hollywood contracts as the same con. Shaan says it worked; Netflix pulled the show.
- Shaan also credits his friend Trevor's "jungle tiger vs zoo tiger" frame for making growth-mindset research memorable. He says memorability is massively underrated: "What's the point of having the good ideas if nobody remembers them?"

chunks.heading: Story is intention, obstacle and a five-second moment of change
chunks.text:
- Shaan learned the core of storytelling from Aaron Sorkin, who said he could teach a "30-second masterclass": intention and obstacle. At any moment you should be able to pause and ask what the character wants and what is in their way. If that is unclear for 5 minutes, attention drifts.
- Intention includes why they want it, how badly, and what happens if they don't get it.
- Stakes don't have to be life or death. He gets "bonus points" for low-stakes moments, and says stories like "I was skiing and there was an avalanche" are unrelatable and even unlikable.
- His example: at an executive offsite after his company was acquired, he told a story about cooking Brussels sprouts for his mom, whom he had never invited over because he didn't know how to host. People came up at the break to say it was hilarious.
- From the book Storyworthy: stakes come from emotion (embarrassment, ego). Don't tell "vacation stories" or "cool party" stories.
- "A story is a five-second moment of change." The ending is the opposite of the opening (rom-coms, Die Hard, Scrooge). The heart of the story is the moment of transformation, usually when the character is cornered or hits rock bottom.
- His advice: if you can't name the five-second moment of change, you don't have a great story yet.
- A story is not a record of what happened. Include events only so far as they explain how the change came about.

chunks.heading: Workshopping an origin story: signature stories and zooming in
chunks.text:
- Shaan recommends having 4-5 "signature stories" (origin story and others) that would tell someone everything about you.
- Workshopping David Perell's origin story, he gave this feedback:
  - Cut details that muddy the message (the raise and promotion didn't fit a story about not doing well).
  - Add concrete low moments that make the "before" state real, such as a performance review where "needs improvement" was far longer than the pros.
  - Don't skip the middle. Explain what triggered the turnaround, the first thing you did, and the resistance you overcame ("you fast-forwarded the montage too fast").
- He cites the Pixar rule that the audience loves the hero for how hard they try, not for winning. An instant success isn't a good story.
- Zoom into moments instead of summarizing, with a visual or audio detail and a feeling. His example is Tony Robbins: washing dishes in the bathtub, one chair, a song playing, then running even though his lungs burned. Robbins has to convince you he was a loser for the "after" to land.
- Self-deprecation and low status build likeability. Hasan Minhaj told him "comedy is a low-status game," and opens a special with his own fertility problem. After a stiff dinner intro, a friend told Shaan to tell a funny story instead of trying to sound impressive.

chunks.heading: Writing mechanics: write like you talk, one reader, emotion first
chunks.text:
- "Write like you talk." He often says the story out loud first, then writes down what he said. Outline by answering: what's the story, what makes it interesting, where does it start, where does it end.
- He uses voice transcription and walks while he talks to get first drafts down.
- School teaches you to pretend (big vocabulary, page minimums). In the real world, good writing is simple, easy to read, entertaining and has a voice.
- Length is only as long as it is interesting. Match it to your buy-in with the audience: on a podcast you can riff, but cold traffic needs a strong headline and first line. TikTok gives under a second.
- Write to one person at one moment. He cites Steve Bartlett's "Jenny in her bedroom" and BuzzFeed's "Debbie at her desk" (the bored-at-work network).
- Work backwards from emotion. Chris Quigley's agency had about an 8-in-10 viral hit rate with this method; Shaan says people only share things that are "LOL, WTF, OMG, AW." Pick the reaction, write to it, then check if it will create it, and juice it up.
- From Gary Halbert's Boron Letters, he took the habit of writing to one specific person you have a warm relationship with (a student, a little cousin, a younger self). Sometimes he plays the sensei; sometimes the beginner who admits "you probably know four better ways."
- He addresses the questions he thinks the reader has at that moment, like a good podcast host would.
- "Imitate, then innovate": deconstruct a favorite writer, find the general principle, then apply it.
- Not everything needs a story. "Comedy is great but not every line should be a joke."

chunks.heading: State, curiosity and getting unstuck
chunks.text:
- He cites Miss Excel, who says she changes her energy before making content, because "all content is energy transferred through the phone." Shaan says no athlete or performer goes on cold, yet most writers start cold.
- Changing your state has three levers:
  - Physiology: sprints, push-ups, air squats, cold water. His poker-pro friend does wind sprints in the parking lot during tournament breaks.
  - Focus: put your attention on what you want, not on the deadline or the difficulty.
  - Story: what you tell yourself. Moving from "I'm doing David a favor" to "one person will hear one thing that changes their life" changes the words that come out.
- He once got out of a writing slump after a coach pointed out that his story had become "I want to be a creative force." What had worked before was finding an interesting idea, figuring it out, and sharing it.
- He quotes Paul Graham: excitement is the engine and the rudder. When he drifted to ambition or money as the driver, things went worse.
- He holds opposing traits together (creative and analytical, visionary and detail-obsessed like Steve Jobs). "If you're in your head, you're dead" is a life philosophy about being present, not a ban on analysis. Use logic for logic problems and emotion for emotion problems.
- To get unstuck: if you're stuck in specifics, go general ("what am I really trying to do?"). If you're stuck in the general, go specific ("what was the best idea I heard in the last 2 days?"). He cites Ray Bradbury's "Don't think" sign.

chunks.heading: Practice, learning from other fields, and building a binge bank
chunks.text:
- He looks for valuable skills that people don't practice or are embarrassed to say they work on: storytelling, enthusiasm, humor, energy. He paid $5,000 to a personal-branding consultant and calls it "the lamest thing ever," but took a useful lesson from it.
- Learn from the masters of the craft (Sorkin, Chappelle, Minhaj, Mr. Beast, Steve Bartlett), not from business people. Mr. Beast studies TV and movie character development because looking only at other YouTubers leads to "a sea of sameness."
- Expect about 100 reps. Do 100 and improve one thing each time. Mr. Beast gives the same advice: make 100 videos, improving one thing each time. Shaan says most people never do it, and those who do never need to come back.
- Create a "binge bank." Two young creators told him each video gets few views, but they are stacking material so anyone curious about them can spend an hour and leave respecting them. He says this beats a resume or portfolio, and it is a way to stay motivated when feedback is small.
- Distribution is earned over time, via the "1-2-3 rule of interestingness" from his friend Jason. One interesting thing is "interesting," two is "those were interesting," three is "you're interesting." On the internet it may take about 20. Seed the first readers with friends, group chats, and personalized messages.
- On Twitter he reached about 400,000 followers. He says he ignored the usual advice (consistency, a niche) and would likely have a million if he had followed it. What worked was having an interesting take when attention was on a subject (his metaverse thread, written when Facebook rebranded to Meta). He says you need two skills: interesting things to say and packaging.

chunks.heading: Brand as a feeling, editing, humor and training a writer
chunks.text:
- Personal brand lesson: "People will follow you to the ends of the earth if you are giving them a feeling that they can't get anywhere else more consistently than anybody else." Examples: TED sells inspiration, comedy podcasts sell camaraderie, Twitch sells the feeling of playing without playing. Pick the feeling, then deliver it consistently.
- Editing process, learned from Sam Parr: write a rough draft, then walk away for roughly 4-24 hours (workout, kids, walk) before editing. When you return, ask whether it does what you wanted and what's blocking it.
- His mindset: it's a river and your ideas are good; remove the rocks. He says Pixar frames each draft as removing the suck.
- Humor:
  - It is the sauce, not the entree.
  - All humor is surprise: set an expectation, then subvert it. He cites Seinfeld's New York Times piece (pooper-scooper streets, towed car, "the greatest place I've ever been").
  - Funny words matter ("pooper scooper").
  - A Theo Von exercise is to rename one thing six different ways ("Jesus' binder").
  - Add a little of the opposite emotion, like Tabasco.
  - His strategy: "pretty smart, kind of funny" beats being the funniest or smartest.
- At Milk Road, a crypto newsletter, he trained a writer who had never written professionally by:
  - Using a consistent format and breaking down the opening line by line, with 10 examples of good.
  - Starting every issue with the same opening pattern (a joke tag like a toaster strudel comparison, "second best feeling in the world... the dolphin hand out the car window").
  - Having him send a voice memo about the news before writing. If it isn't interesting in a voice note, it won't be interesting in text, which filters out topics you're not truly interested in.
  - Making the goal "give you a reason to open this that's not based on the Bitcoin price."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan, interviewed by his former intern, shares philosophies from before he made money: optimize for freedom and learning over cash, move close to what you want, pick projects and partners over grinding, and only do work that is its own reward. Packed with stories (sushi startup, Mr. Beast's 100 videos, selling Bebo).

chunks.heading: Pick projects and partners before effort: hard work is overrated
chunks.text:
- Shaan says "hard work is overrated." He ranks it maybe the fourth or fifth most important variable, behind project selection, who you work with, timing and luck.
- Project selection comes first. "Choosing what you work on is far more important than how hard you work." He notes that in the restaurant industry, no amount of effort changes your outcomes much.
- He thinks successful people credit hard work because it "sounds good" and gives them air cover. It implies everyone had an equal shot.
- Hard work is still good for building skill and showing you are serious. In your 20s you can throw hours at problems. As you get older, have kids and have less energy, your judgment has to make up for the lost time.
- Most projects fail but the skills stick. His sushi restaurant failed, but along the way he learned After Effects, iMovie and Photoshop "just enough to be dangerous." That helped him mock things up himself in Silicon Valley.
- Skills can't be inherited, bought or taken away. He paraphrases Derek Sivers on this. Skill is "the key that unlocks an infinite number of doors."
- Skill transfer example: a founder who learned paid ads in small DTC e-commerce moved to a venture-backed B2B software company. Most people there were 0 to 6 out of 10 at paid ads, so it was "shooting fish in a barrel." He was selling a $20,000 recurring contract instead of a $20 widget, and the company hit a roughly $300-400M valuation within two years.
- Picking projects and picking partners are both skills. Few people even use the phrase "project selection."

chunks.heading: Choose a project by whether the work itself is the reward
chunks.text:
- His rule now: "Am I doing this for a result or because I like doing it?" He no longer works on something for a future payoff.
- "The work has to be the win." The result becomes a bonus. If you do it for the payoff and it fails, which is most of the time, you have wasted the time.
- He spent 10 years doing things only because of "ooh, if this worked it'd be amazing." He believes he'd be further ahead had he followed enjoyment earlier, though you can't A/B test a life.
- The flywheel: you enjoy it, so you do it all the time. Doing it all the time makes you really good. Being really good gets the results. Without enjoyment you only work as hard as your willpower allows, you get so-so good, and you get a so-so result.
- He cites Paul Graham's idea to let "interestingness" be the filter. Your taste profile can't be copied, so it filters out other people, and it keeps you doing the work.
- The cost to avoid is opportunity cost, which is bigger than taxes or expenses for anyone smart enough.

chunks.heading: Find your thing: ask other people and audit your five-to-nine
chunks.text:
- Other people spot your strengths before you do. His example is Naval, who wanted to be a physicist. His mom said he was a business guy because he kept pointing out how restaurants could raise revenue or change their menus.
- Ask friends: "What's my superpower? What comes easy to me that's harder for other people?"
- Ask yourself where you do things that feel like play to you but look like work or a grind to others. Look at your five-to-nine, not your nine-to-five, and at what you do beyond what is rational.
- His own example: before a recording he was reading the Nevada annual report on Las Vegas Strip casino revenues for 2024 vs 2023, as a possible recession indicator. Nobody assigned it. Years of those rabbit holes became the library of facts and stories he uses on the podcast.
