- As a kid he never played NBA 2K games. He ran franchise mode, scouting players, making trades and raising concession prices. That was practice at being a manager or CEO.
- Don't hide or fix your oddities. Ask what superpower they give you and where they would be valuable.
- His wife is OCD and loved arts and crafts. She started bedazzling phones with Swarovski crystals, and as a freshman celebrities were asking for custom pieces and she was making thousands of dollars a month.

chunks.heading: Be serious: the rule of 100 and the competition thinning out
chunks.text:
- At a Tony Robbins event, a Simon Says game among 10,000 people ended with five on stage. When asked, only about 50 people had believed they would win. Shaan's takeaway is that you were competing with 50, "not 10,000." Most people are not serious, so if you are, your odds are much better than they look.
- Jimmy Donaldson (MrBeast) tells would-be YouTubers to make 100 videos, improving one thing each time (intro, caption, outro, music, pacing, editing). Then come back and he'll say what's next.
- Nobody comes back. Jimmy says that by 100 videos they no longer need him because they have momentum.
- Jimmy himself posted for roughly seven years with almost nobody watching before it took off. Shaan says the rule of 100 applies to any pursuit.
- Everything Jimmy does is public and has been for a decade, yet people still ask for the secret.

chunks.heading: Proximity is power and network selection
chunks.text:
- From Tony Robbins: proximity is power. "Pull, not push." If everyone you like and respect works out, it is almost easier to do it than to resist.
- Poker example: the people who got good lived in a house with five other obsessed players, ate and slept poker and reviewed hands at dinner. They improved far faster than others. Same logic as learning Spanish by living in Mexico instead of using Duolingo.
- He moved to San Francisco for startups. Three times he asked who the most impressive founder was, and each time they had already moved there. He changed his phone number to a San Francisco area code, told people he was moving, only job hunted there, signed a lease and flew in on a one-way ticket.
- James Currier (NFX, roughly a $1.2B fund) pushes the network view. Where you go to college is a network you join. Moving to cheaper taxes can be a dumb trade if you leave the "white hot center" of tech or AI. For good people, opting into a better network is almost always worth more than the incremental dollar, especially early, because it compounds.
- He told his former intern that a sales job at about $12k a month would put him "another sales guy," and that working with him would be the better network. He admits this was a mistake of the same kind he made early on.
- Your info diet is also a network. If you consume what everyone else consumes you'll think what they think. To differentiate, change your info diet, the people you spend time with and what you do in your free time. Jiu-jitsu is one example of a different hobby that opts you into a different network.
- Better does not mean you can't win elsewhere. It means higher odds and an easier path. "There's no bonus points for doing everything the hard way."

chunks.heading: Partner selection: Buffett's three plus "down"
chunks.text:
- Buffett's framework is energy, intelligence and integrity. Without integrity you get a smart crook. Without intelligence you don't get anywhere.
- Shaan adds a fourth: being "down." It is his highest priority. Down means:
  - willing to try a half-baked idea
  - up for adventure over the safe path
  - willing to buckle down and grind without running from difficulty
- Example: Ben (now his business partner) had a SaaS business making about $1M a year in profit. Shaan asked him to spend time on a random project with only a rough idea. Ben said he was down. They have done five to seven things together since, and every one has been fun and has worked.

chunks.heading: Strategically broke year and the sushi restaurant
chunks.text:
- After college he took a $120,000 a year job in a boring industry. A month and a half in he quit, because his group had won a business plan competition for a sushi chain idea, Sabi Sushi ("the Chipotle of sushi"), with $25,000 in prize money for the three of them. That was about $8,000 each for a year.
- He chose to be "strategically broke." His banker friends were money rich and time poor. He chose to be time rich, adventure rich and learning rich instead, learning 12 times more to match the 12x income gap.
- What he learned: P&Ls, margins, pitching investors, lease negotiation, real estate, sales, marketing, design, video editing, blogging, hiring and firing.
- Negotiation example: he found that a liquor license puts a lease on file with the city. He looked up what a restaurant with a license paid, then negotiated his own rent down using that figure.
- Lifestyle was minimal: an air mattress and a garbage bag nailed to the wall as a bin.
- Side income: coaching basketball at a school for autistic children and tutoring stats at $25-30 an hour. He calculated the minimum he needed to earn for maximum freedom.
- He applies the same principle now. He works out the minimum funding a company needs to reach its next milestone, such as 1,000 customers who love it. He asks what amount of money feels good while leaving the most time for family and projects.
- He quotes Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot) that his first business, run by ignorance, did better than his second, and that "just because I was ignorant doesn't mean I was wrong."
- He quit the sushi restaurant too, as it did not work out.

chunks.heading: Reversing decisions, motion over direction, and quitting the wrong thing
chunks.text:
- Shaan says he is not good at making decisions but is "great at reversals." Once he sees a decision is wrong he cuts it off fast, he says partly because he can't tolerate it.
- Underneath most reasons for staying is fear: of rejection, embarrassment, failure. People use code words like "stress." Many would "rather live in pain than go toward an unknown."
- His dad backed the sushi plan, even calling it a terrible idea, because Shaan was newly switched on and building skills. The analogy: you're on a foggy beach and want paradise but can't see it. You can wait for the fog to clear or paddle out in your small boat. Once you're moving it is easy to change direction, so "sometimes life is about motion, not direction."
- Selling Bebo (his company, run in a lab funded by a billionaire): the office was the nicest in San Francisco, with a private chef, a Friday masseuse and a built-in bar. A friend, Sully, told him over a casino buffet at 1 a.m., "I don't get what you're doing." Six years in, the project was neither a success nor an obvious failure.
- Sully's inertia test, the thought experiment: if the lab closed tomorrow, would you call the same people and start this same thing? Shaan realised the answer was no.
- The next day he told his co-founder to sell the company or end it. He asked the investor for 30 days to sell it or he'd walk away and hand over his equity. They signed a definitive agreement about 45 days later, with diligence still to come.
- The ideal answer to "would I be doing this if I weren't already?" is a "hell yes." Tweaks, like the commute, are fine to fix. He borrows from Elon: "The biggest waste of time is doing something well that needn't have been done at all."
- Mediocrity is the real risk for high-potential people: "it'll sap your will, your time, your resources, your energy, your belief in yourself." Failure is quick and keeps your time at your disposal.

chunks.heading: Make life intentional: Misogi
chunks.text:
- A Misogi (from Jesse Itzler, who was a podcast guest) is one grand challenge each year that is hard, memorable and meaningful. Shaan wants one so years don't blend together. Time otherwise fills with Zoom calls, errands and weekly stand-ups.
- His 2025 Misogi was learning to play the piano well enough to jam, and to play in a "dad band."
- He wants to be able to play for the rest of his life, including at 80.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan Puri argues project selection and who you work with matter far more than hard work. He calls enthusiasm and storytelling underrated skills, says to change your state by acting rather than thinking, and warns most people learn the wrong lesson from failure.

chunks.heading: Project selection beats hard work
chunks.text:
- Shaan calls hard work "massively overrated" and ranks it fourth or fifth in importance. Number one is what you work on; number two is who you work with.
- Hard work is a threshold, not a differentiator. Going from 40 to 70 to 90 hours a week matters far less than people think.
- His example: restaurant cooks and janitors work the hardest of anyone, yet "hard work will let you win the game that you're playing but it doesn't help you if you chose the wrong game."
- He criticizes school for forcing a major at 17 or 18 with no preparation. Picking the project is the highest-leverage decision, and it is treated as a throwaway.
- Simple decisions that take little time can separate success from failure. He calls himself "somewhat lazy but very happy and successful."
- He says hard work is overrated partly because it is virtue signaling. Genetics, birthplace and resources are out of your control, so people credit the one visible choice they made.
- People credit themselves for wins and blame luck or the economy for losses.
- He rejects the "no self-made man" idea as true but not useful. His rule: "pick the ones that serve you."

chunks.heading: Enthusiasm as an underrated skill
chunks.text:
- At 24 he joined a Silicon Valley company of about 20 people as the youngest, with no coding or design skill. His edge was enthusiasm: painting a picture that excites him, then sprinting at it.
- He defines enthusiasm as borrowing happiness and excitement from the future and deploying it today. It matters most when things are neutral or bad, because most hard things have deep dips.
- Silicon Valley rewards optimism: "the cynics get to be right and the optimists get to be rich." Cynics are right on the eight of ten startups that fail and miss the two that work.
- Set your emotional home near ten, not zero. Many smart people deliberately start at neutral. He cites a Conor McGregor line: "you got to feel some type of way so why not feel unbeatable."
- Vicious cycle: low belief leads to minimal action, then a minimal result, which reinforces the belief. The virtuous cycle is the reverse. Enthusiasm lifts default belief, then action, then results.
- Tactic: "honey I'm home" energy. Before walking into a meeting or your home, decide to enter with that high energy. Hold it for about 45 seconds and people respond differently. Relationships fade when the early-days enthusiasm dips.

chunks.heading: Storytelling: intention, obstacle, stakes
chunks.text:
- Stories are the natural transfer mechanism between people. Religions and The Lion King stick because they are encoded as stories, while seventh-grade lessons do not.
- Almost nobody is taught storytelling, so even a little effort puts you in the top few percent.
- Core principle from Aaron Sorkin's masterclass: "intention and obstacle." A hero wants something and something is in the way. Examples: Die Hard, the show Hijack, a romantic comedy.
- Add stakes to raise the story. Stakes need not be life or death; you only need to convince the audience this matters hugely to the character.
- His example is a low-stakes story told at an executive retreat. He was cooking brussels sprouts for his mom to look like an adult in his first apartment. Everyone else was one-upping each other with fires, and the small story won.

chunks.heading: If you're in your head, you're dead
chunks.text:
- Smart people try to think their way to happiness, which he compares to talking your way through cooking. Thinking won't solve a feeling problem.
- Most people assume think leads to feel leads to do. He argues the loop runs both ways, and acting is the easier lever: do something physical and you feel differently, then think differently.
- Examples: 50 push-ups, a cold plunge, or submerging your face in ice water for a panic attack (a tip from Emmett Shear, citing the mammalian dive reflex).
- Make big decisions while moving, not slumped at a desk eating muffins.

chunks.heading: Mental minimalism and orienting principles
chunks.text:
- He proposes "mental minimalism." Collecting mental models and frameworks like stamps is wasted energy. He prefers a few principles, in the spirit of Bruce Lee's one kick practiced a thousand times.
- The midwit meme (Neanderthal, overcomplicator, Jedi): the simple and the sage answers match. Example: lift weights and eat protein.
- Knowledge is knowing what to do. Wisdom is doing it. People over-index on knowledge and under-index on doing.
- Test he applied to a founder: asked what went wrong at his last company, the founder talked 20 minutes. The answer should be short.
- Pros-and-cons lists tie people in knots. Reduce a decision to one reason.

chunks.heading: Time horizons and why failure teaches less than people claim
chunks.text:
- Change a decision by shrinking or stretching its time frame. Shrink it ("what's the best I can do in 45 minutes?") or stretch it ("I want to do awesome things with awesome people long-term").
- Story: he missed three deals that became billion-dollar companies because he had no money. He then asked how to invest without money, did a deal with an older friend and took less economics. The friend texted that he didn't care about the deal and wanted to do deals for 20 years. Long-term orientation changes behavior.
- A friend's "worry time": worry about money only Sunday 11am to noon, which frees you the rest of the week. His trainer's version: "you don't plant the seed and then dig it up the next day."
- He doubts "I failed but I learned." Ask what they learned and most can't say, or learn the wrong lesson.
- Example: a young employee bought a delisted stock, doubled down and got lucky. The takeaway for the kid was "I'm a genius" rather than "I got lucky."
- Memory of your own thoughts is poor, so keep a system. Write down your reasoning at decision time, then review it later. Judgment is the most important skill and can be trained this way.

chunks.heading: Being a billionaire is a stupid goal
chunks.text:
- Billionaires give most of it away, which signals that abundance beyond a point doesn't matter.
- His own money checkpoints: not having to work because investments cover you, and getting out of debt.
- Past about $50M versus $500M, the difference is minor ("one rents the jet, the other owns the jet").
- Prefer abundance in time, youth, energy, freedom, generosity and fun. At 21 he wanted what 40-year-olds had; at 35 he wants what 21-year-olds have.
- He picked his path by asking who is having the most fun in their career. He found it hard to name people at a "10." Many successful people are stuck at "seven" and don't know there is a higher setting.
- Joe Rogan example: turned his hobbies into work (UFC commentary, comedy, podcasting) while avoiding the traps, such as constant touring, a content treadmill and censoring himself. Pick goals and also "anti-goals."
- Cautionary tale: a college friend's father made $1M a year as a consulting partner but traveled Monday to Thursday for her whole life, and she resented it.

chunks.heading: Spend on services, not things
chunks.text:
- Season of life: from Bill Perkins's *Die With Zero*, a friend quit to backpack Europe at about 22-25, while Perkins stayed and went at 33, when it was less fun. Do things when they have maximum impact.
- Most people buy luxury goods. Shaan says services beat experiences and experiences beat things.
- He hired a private chef for less than a luxury car costs, and an assistant (via Shepherd, based in the Philippines) for about the cost of a couple of purses. The assistant screens email, handles his calendar, and helps him be a better friend by sending gifts and tracking birthdays.
- His rule on others' wealth: treat it like Costco samples. After he got defensive about a Las Vegas mansion, a friend called out his bitterness. He now treats exposure to other lifestyles as a cheap way to learn what he wants and doesn't want.
- He and a friend agreed to give each other blunt feedback and receive it "as a gift."
- Heuristic: don't follow what most people do, because the average outcome (obesity, divorce, no savings) isn't one you want.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan and his business partner Ben Levy explain how they pick a new mission every 3-6 months, treat luck as a metric you track, and build relationships through lightweight texts plus long in-person hangs. They also riff on half-baked ideas like rebranding ugly categories and paid hardship experiences.

chunks.heading: Treat luck as a skill you can measure and manage
chunks.text:
- Shaan and Ben have worked together for 5 years and created nine projects that each made over $1M.
- He argues luck is something you can influence: "we actually treat like creating luck as a skill."
- Applying Peter Drucker's "what gets measured gets managed," Ben keeps a "luck sheet." Each day he logs the 5-6 things he did to create luck, then logs which ones later paid off (a tweet that became MFM content, a deal he chased and wired into, a hire, an intro).
- The annual goal for Ben is 100 lucky breaks, which takes roughly 500-700 interesting actions.
- Shaan traced the best outcomes of the last two years "like 23andMe, ancestry.com." Each key customer, intro and hire for a business that crossed $10M ARR, profitable and bootstrapped, in under 18 months came from "Ben doing random [stuff]."
- Measuring it changes decisions. It gives the green light to shoot shots, like flying out for 2 days to hang with Jesse Itzler with no agenda.
- Most attempts lead nowhere, and that is fine. None of it is transactional; the goal is to be useful.

chunks.heading: The relationship-guy model (the Nick Dio / Gary Vee idea)
chunks.text:
- Nick Dio is Gary Vee's relationship guy: he hosts dinners, takes people on trips and hangs out with people Gary likes, often without Gary there.
- Shaan compares it to LeBron spending about $1M a year on his body. His version is "what's my version of spending a million dollars a year on my body," meaning the business asset is relationships.
- Gary builds a magnet with his content, but he can't personally meet everyone it attracts, so he hired someone to do it.
- Shaan is an introvert who creates content from his bedroom. Ben is extroverted, replies to everyone, checks in, and congratulates people on milestones (for example sending a cake with their number on it).
- Why it works: the extrovert turns the content's attraction into relationships. Roughly 1 in 20 people ends up teaching them something, becoming an investment, or helping in another way.

chunks.heading: The barbell for relationships: light touch or long hang
chunks.text:
- The model is a barbell of two extremes: constant lightweight texting (memes, tweets, quick notes), or long in-person time.
- Shaan, relaying an idea from John Coogan, says the middle is death: "death by a thousand Zoom calls." A 40-45 minute Zoom costs energy but builds little depth or bond.
- A 5-hour hang (lunch, walk, coffee) is worth far more, "the equivalent of like 200 Zoom calls."
- Example: Chris Sacca moved out of San Francisco to Truckee, bought a cabin plus a guest house, and invited interesting founders for 48-hour weekends (hot tub, skiing, cooking, talking). That is how he got into Uber and Instagram: he understood the founders and businesses in depth and knew to "back up the truck."
- Going to someone's home also shows how they live and whether you want that life.

chunks.heading: Find your "first believer"
chunks.text:
- Shaan says everyone successful had someone who irrationally believed in them before there was proof. His was Michael Burch, who gave him the CEO job around age 23-24 when he wasn't qualified.
- He calls it belief as an angel investor, before money. It matters more than cash as a starting ingredient.
- How they pay it forward: they say it out loud. They text people they believe in ("I'm buying all the Billy Oppenheimer stock on the market right now"). Shaan also suggests thanking whoever believed in you.
- How Ben and Shaan started: Ben was a listener in a CEO mastermind group Shaan ran (a test that became Sam Parr's Hampton). Ben's business had one customer, Anheuser-Busch, paying about $1M a year. Ben was bored, had hit a wall growing it, and said yes to a 90-day project.
- That led to the All Access Pass, which did over $1M. For 90 days Shaan emailed subscribers daily what he worked on while building a business (an ecom brand, a fund, a course).

chunks.heading: Pick a 3-6 month "main mission" and learn from a curated peer group
chunks.text:
- Shaan and Ben choose a main mission roughly every 3-6 months (longest 1-2 years): raise a fund (about $20M raised for startup investing), grow his ecom brand (from about $5M to $25-30M in revenue over about 12 months), grow MFM, and so on.
- Neither knew ecom, so Ben built "Club LTV": a free, curated group of ecom owners doing over $5M in revenue who met every other Friday.
- Format: speed-dating style intros and one founder presenting what's working (TikTok, email), with groups reshuffled.
- It drew about 150 owners in the first month. Any problem they had, someone in the group had already solved.
- The plan to bring it back: a free, curated group of the top 1% of MFM's roughly 1 million listeners ("entrepreneurs with a sense of humor"), meeting monthly in shuffled groups. Shared fandom makes people likely to get along.

chunks.heading: Half-baked ideas with real mechanics
chunks.text:
- **Courtside YouTube channel:** buy courtside seats and interview a different person each game (what they do, how they make money). Estimated cost is about $100K in Orlando and $400-500K in New York. Shaan thinks sponsors like FanDuel or SeatGeek could fund part of it. He'd also pay about $20 a month for a service that identifies who sits courtside, a "business meets basketball" paparazzi.
- **Lunch bounty marketplace:** people bid on a one-hour lunch with a notable person and proceeds go to the person's chosen charity. It could be launched permissionlessly and use public pressure. Reference points: Monish Pabrai paid $650K for lunch with Warren Buffett. At two lunches a week averaging about $25K, it raises about $2.5M for charity.
- **"Everyone needs their Birkin bag":** collectibles are huge (Whatnot, live pack-opening commerce, is valued at about $5B and has done about $5B in sales; Shaan and Ben missed the chance to invest at about $50-60M). Open question: which niche doesn't have its Birkin yet. Shaan likes tech collectibles and one-of-one musician pieces.
- **Real-life Survivor:** for "post-economic" people (making money no longer drives decisions) who crave voluntary hardship and digital detox. Shaan says $10K with about 20 people living as a tribe is more scalable, like the new Tough Mudder. The same logic applies to a Love Is Blind pods tour.
- **Coach K in a box:** AI-made custom motivational videos for a workout or sales call. Shaan's version of the story: Coach K's locker-room videos spliced Braveheart-style footage with your own game film.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan shares how he learned audience-building from Bebo and Steven Bartlett's theme-page "Thunder Clap", why podcasts are the hardest audience to grow, and his "trust equation" for valuing audiences. He also covers how to choose projects, stay patient with results, and decide when to quit.

chunks.heading: Why podcasts are the hardest audience to grow
chunks.text:
Shaan names this as the hardest thing he has promoted. He uses Eric Ries's three engines of growth (from The Lean Startup) to explain why.

- **Viral engine:** "Using your product naturally spreads like a contagion." Podcasts are "the ultimate single player experience". They are a one-hour solo listen in headphones, so they don't spread the way music does at gyms or parties.
- **Paid engine:** it works when you put money in and get more money out, as e-commerce brands do with Facebook ads. Podcasts fail here because there is nowhere obvious to advertise, conversion is low, and the ad revenue arrives later and is small compared to acquisition cost.
- **Sticky engine:** the only one left. People who really use you stay, engagement deepens, and they eventually tell others voluntarily. He calls it "annual compound interest of like 5%", so "you gotta get rich slow".
- Early on, low feedback is a strength. Nobody can see your view count, so you aren't discouraged. Guests will also come on with 100 listeners because they can't see the numbers.
- Later it becomes a weakness, because you want the feedback loop. MFM pushes people to YouTube even though it earns less there than from audio downloads. He wants the best product, and comments let him learn and re-engage.

chunks.heading: The trust equation: audience quality × size × trust
chunks.text:
Shaan rejects size as the main audience metric. He maximizes a "trust equation":

- Trust equation = quality of the audience × number of those people × how much they trust you.
- One view or listen is not equal to another. A teenager on TikTok is not the same viewer as a company CEO.
- TikTok can give huge numbers but only seven seconds of attention before a swipe. Hours of long-form content builds far more trust.
- For creators, he says to choose "the right 10,000" who trust you a lot and stack the number slowly. That beats a random 100,000.
- For marketers, the arbitrage is finding assets that are underpriced because their trust is higher than their headline number.

chunks.heading: Twitch streamers and G Fuel: buying trust cheaply
chunks.text:
Shaan saw this while at Twitch, which acquired his first company.

- Traditional brand marketers judged creators by Instagram followers or YouTube subscribers.
- A Twitch streamer is live in their bedroom, unedited and unscripted, six to eight hours a day. Twitch is 10-20x smaller than YouTube or Instagram as a network, but watch time is comparable, and that builds enormous trust.
- Big brands held back because execs didn't understand Twitch, couldn't track clicks, or feared a streamer saying the wrong thing.
- G Fuel (a Red Bull / Monster-style energy drink) went to about five streamers, then:
  - Gave each their own branded shaker, with the streamer's face on it, in a different colour for each.
  - Spent nothing beyond that.
  - Went from zero to $40 million in sales in about 12 months.
- Shaan says the same underpricing was true of podcasters a few years earlier, and he calls it "less so" now for both. He uses the same approach to grow Milk Road and his e-commerce business today.

chunks.heading: The "no link, complain about it" Thunder Clap launch
chunks.text:
This is the launch tactic Steven Bartlett used at Shaan's company, which Shaan describes in detail.

- Bartlett had built a network of themed meme pages (Freshman Problems, Harry Potter memes, overheard-on-campus accounts). He bought pages for around $1,000 or partnered with their teenage owners.
- For the app launch, every page posted on the same day, which they called a Thunder Clap.
- The rules were:
  - No links. A kid once told Shaan "links are gay", and Bartlett had the same instinct that a link instantly makes a post look like an ad.
  - Don't praise the product, because that also sounds like selling.
  - Complain about it instead, such as "I haven't gotten anything done today because I'm so addicted to this stupid app" or "if one more friend tells me to download X, I'm gonna lose it".
- Followers saw the same unknown app three times on one scroll and went to the App Store to search the name.
- The result was about 500,000 downloads in roughly five days with no marketing spend, and #1 in the entire free App Store.
- Shaan's takeaways:
  - How you talk about a product matters. Fake-authentic, curiosity-building talk beats pushing a product at people.
  - The app churned users after about 10 days, so the distribution method was worth more than the app. Bartlett went on to build the agency Social Chain from it.
  - Bartlett's personal vlog content was aimed at the right audience, not a big one. Each client was worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, so paying a camera person to follow him was a good investment.

chunks.heading: Two failed audience hacks first
chunks.text:
Shaan says people know My First Million but not his earlier false starts.

- Attempt one: he bought the failed social network Bebo back out of bankruptcy for about $1 million, planning to relaunch a different product under the name and its press story. It failed.
- Attempt two: he and Bartlett cold-called Logan Paul's manager, but Logan's team wanted a lot of money and they passed.
- The Thunder Clap only came after those. The actual value from Bebo was that it attracted Bartlett, who cold-emailed to work for him.
- He chose podcast, Twitter and newsletter because he is not a charismatic on-camera personality like Bartlett and wanted a medium that suits him ("a face for podcasting").
- Results he cites:
  - Podcast: 20 million+ downloads a year.
  - Newsletters: hundreds of thousands of subscribers.
  - Twitter: about 400,000 followers.
  - Those audiences let him spin off multiple businesses earning millions in profit.

chunks.heading: Project selection and starting with a kickoff doc
chunks.text:
Shaan says what you choose to work on matters more than how hard you work.

- He failed for his first eight years of entrepreneurship. His learning came from "trial and error" done intelligently. Years of doing the same thing do not count as improvement. "It's the rate of learning and the rate of improvement that matters."
- He writes a one-page "kickoff doc" before any project to get clarity on what he is trying to do.
- He started the podcast the day after selling his company, after a 4-hour walk through the Mission in San Francisco. He wanted to be "in a million people's earballs in the morning", like Tim Ferriss.
- His stated downside was to lose $10,000 and have 100 great conversations, with the upside of accidentally building an audience. He also disliked asking people for coffee meetings, so a podcast invitation replaced them.
- Questions he asks to judge a project:
  - If you knew you'd be paid $5 million a year regardless, what would you do? This strips away the variable rewards of success odds and money.
  - Would you keep doing it if it never grew? He says yes for the podcast, which is why he knew it was right.
  - If the logical reasons say don't but you still want to, lean in. An immediate payoff beats a future one.
- Audience-first only makes sense if you actually like the content creation. He says it is no easier than building a product directly, only different, and many people give up because they expect it to be faster.
- Mindset quote from Naval: "Impatience with action, patience with results." Beginners expect things to happen faster than they do.

chunks.heading: When to quit a project
chunks.text:
Shaan's own bias is to quit sooner, but from investing in about 100 startups and talking to thousands of founders, he thinks most people stick with things too long.

- "Quitting is underrated." Time is finite and projects are infinite.
- Survivorship bias distorts perseverance stories. He calls Pinterest's founder changing Apple Store laptop homepages "great story, terrible advice".
- His process:
  1. Before starting, talk to people who have done it. Look at the average successful journey, not the average including failures, so you know how long it takes. Check whether you even want their day-to-day.
  2. Set a worry time (a concept from Justin Mares). Plant the seed, water it for about 90 days, then assess, rather than digging it up daily.
  3. If you keep going against the evidence, say so out loud and don't delude yourself.
  4. After roughly six months to a year, ask: knowing what I know now, do I believe more, less or the same that this is valuable, that it is possible, and that my method gets me there? The answer should rarely be "the same".
- Don't be held hostage by your initial conviction. He expects to be wrong more than half the time.
- He warns that "marketers are great at bullshitting" and must be careful not to market to themselves.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan explains how to find a career you'll stick with through the "decade of suck": test-drive jobs before committing, take a time-boxed season of wandering, and hunt for clues (energy and blueprints). Love is framed as a competitive advantage because people who love it practice more.

chunks.heading: Test-drive the dream before committing to it
chunks.text:
- Shaan argues that whatever job you think you want is "probably wrong," because most people name a career because it sounded good to friends, parents and college counselors.
- His rule: "Try before you buy." Take a 2-week test drive of the job instead of letting the dream "float in a magical theoretical bubble."
- His own case: he spent 10 years saying he wanted to be a sports medicine doctor. He met an orthopedic surgeon for a sports team at a wedding and asked to shadow him for 2 weeks. He learned right away that he did not want the job because it has very little creativity.
- The lesson he drew: creativity and variety matter a lot to him. Those 2 weeks saved him from 8 years of med school and another 20-30 years in a job that "didn't light me up."
- Possible outcomes of a test drive:
  - **Yes**: invest a decade becoming great at it.
  - **No**: glad to find out now.
  - **Maybe**: treat it as a no, citing Derek Sivers: "if it's not a Hell Yes, it's a No".

chunks.heading: Why the "decade of suck" is survivable only if you like the game
chunks.text:
- Shaan describes his early years as roughly 10-12 years of flat-line progress before the big upswing that everyone focuses on.
- His claim: people don't get through that stretch on willpower alone (unless they are David Goggins). The ones who make it enjoy the game and "play to play" rather than "play to win."
- They keep going while friends get promotions and buy houses, even when "the scoreboard says: Life 12, You 0."
- They keep playing until they get so good "the game has no choice but to give them the win."
- This is why he says to find a game you love. Loving it is the only thing that sustains the repetitions.

chunks.heading: Give yourself a "season of wandering"
chunks.text:
- High achievers get anxious without an answer for their life, so they prematurely commit to something, anything. He cites Tim Ferriss: most people would rather be unhappy than uncertain.
- The fix is to name the era and time-box it. His reasoning: people behave differently when something has a name and a date (he points to Mardi Gras and Burning Man).
- He calls it a "season of wandering": 3 to 12 months where you experiment, dabble, try things and follow your curiosity and excitement.
- He calls it "wandering" because it lets you think creatively. There is no wrong path as long as you follow curiosity.
- What to look for while wandering: "clues, not answers." Like a detective, you don't seek the answer directly; answers come from clues.
- His closing argument for permission: most people say they can't afford the time, money or courage, but "you only get one ride on this rollercoaster," so the better question is whether you can afford not to.

chunks.heading: Clue 1: energy, and "play to you, work to others"
chunks.text:
- Track what gives you energy versus what drains you. His examples: he gets drained at social events and gets tons of energy from reading books.
- The sharper test: "what feels like play to you, but looks like work to others?" He calls that the moneymaker.
- His example is writing. Most people hate it and dread the blank page, but he loves it.
- He followed that clue to Milk Road, a newsletter company. A year later it had 250,000 subscribers and sold for millions of dollars.
- His thesis: "Energy is the key to success," not hard work. His energy comes from loving what he does rather than grinding harder.
- Why love is a competitive advantage: people who love it do it more, the more you practice the better you get, and the better you get the more money you make.
- His definition of a great career: doing things you love, with people you love.

chunks.heading: Clue 2: find blueprints
chunks.text:
- He quotes Tony Robbins: "Success leaves clues." The fastest shortcut in self-improvement is to find someone who already has what you want and download their habits and mindset.
- The question to ask: "Who's living the life I want?" Be specific about what "the life" means.
- His own example of refining the blueprint: he wanted success, then met rich men who were busy, stressed and divorced, with kids who resented them. He updated the target to money and fun and a house full of love, then sought out people who had all three.
- When he found someone matching that profile he drilled in with two questions: what do they do, and how did they get started?

chunks.heading: Get outside your bubble: there are 10,000x more ways to win
chunks.text:
- Examples of unexpected paths he ran into:
  - A man who got very rich selling the conveyor belts that go on treadmills.
  - An older ping-pong friend who imports fancy soaps from Italy and resells them to 5-star hotels at a big markup, making $3M a year. He doesn't make the soap; "he just saw a gap and filled it."
- His takeaway: there are 10,000x more ways to win than you realize. You may not do any of them, but they open your eyes to possibilities.
- His parents had normal 9-to-5 jobs, so they could only teach him that flavor. His line: "you can't ask someone for directions to a place they've never been."
- Instead of complaining about his upbringing, he moved to SF because he wanted to be a founder and that's where founders live: "Proximity is power."
- His result: he gets paid to talk (his podcast), has built and sold multiple companies, and works on whatever he wants, whenever and from wherever he wants. He says he'd do podcasting, writing and investing for free.

chunks.heading: The 3-step plan, and his stance on luck
chunks.text:
- The plan in short:
  - **Pop the bubble**: test drive the job before committing.
  - **Season of wandering**: take 3 to 12 months to experiment and follow curiosity.
  - **Look for clues**: ask what feels like play to you but looks like work to others, and find blueprints in people who already have what you want, then study and hang around them.
- Shaan admits luck matters (he says he "rolled the dice and hit a hard six"), but argues that if you think it's all luck you're a victim of circumstances: "Luck matters, but action matters more."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan explains how he funded a no-job year in his 20s by calculating the minimum money needed for maximum freedom, living cheap, and earning via tutoring, coaching and business plan competition prizes. He then used the time to build "master skills" through low-stakes projects that each sucked a little less.

chunks.heading: Spending a year "strategically broke" after college
chunks.text:
Shaan skipped the post-college job track and made a year of no job, no salary and no plan on purpose. He called it his own "grad school": a year to work on projects, travel, and figure out what he wanted to do. He had heard a line from a guy at a casino 16 years earlier that stuck with him: "I don't know much, but I know one thing: the ordinary life isn't for me." He wanted a creative life, with friends, and to "get filthy rich in the process."

He says the trade was worth it:
- A year of free time in your 20s is worth a decade of free time at 65.
- Skills and relationships built in your 20s have 20+ years to compound.
- Young travel (backpacking, hostels) is easy and cheap. By the 40s it is "damn near impossible", and with a wife and 3 kids it is "more like a U-Haul move, with fist-fulls of diapers."
- "Nice stuff" was cool, but "freedom of time was much cooler."

His tweet on this got 200,000 views. Older people agreed, and younger people asked how to do it without money. He says he didn't want to be "that guy" who tells people money doesn't matter, so he describes what he actually did.

chunks.heading: Living scrappy: the cost structure
chunks.text:
Shaan lived in Boulder, Colorado with two best friends, Trev and Dan. Boulder has outdoors, a university party scene and lots of entrepreneurs (Techstars was based there).

- They rented a bad 2-bedroom apartment for about $1,400 a month, roughly $466 each.
- Trevor slept on an air mattress in the living room, which was also the bedroom, office and gym.
- Furniture was free Craigslist desks and Target air mattresses.
- Their pet was a free mouse named Marty.
- The menu was Costco frozen grilled chicken ($25 for 10 pounds), eggs, avocados (the luxury item), rice, ranch style beans, and "tons" of Frank's Red Hot.

chunks.heading: Calculate the minimum, not the maximum
chunks.text:
Shaan didn't try to maximize income. He "calculated the minimum money needed to live with max freedom."

- He decided he needed about $1,000 a month.
- His goal was to earn that in about 5 hours of work a week.
- He tutored math at $35/hour, first for a girl he met at a bar and then her friends. When she asked if it would be free if she were his girlfriend, he said "I'll take the $35/hour, thanks." His takeaway: "you can't hustle a hustler."
- He coached basketball at a school for autistic children, $35/hour for 2 hours a week.
- These gigs brought in about $700/month for roughly 5 hours a week.

chunks.heading: Getting paid for the pitch: business plan competitions
chunks.text:
Once he hit his 5-hour cap, Shaan asked: "what's something easy I could do once, that would give me my entire year goal?" His belief is that "constraints breed creativity."

- He was already brainstorming business ideas. The shortcut was to pitch the idea and get paid for the pitch, without building the business.
- He found niche business plan competitions with decent prizes and low competition.
- He entered a dozen, got paid by 2, and he and his team won $25K+ in prize money.
- That covered about 2 years of living costs.

chunks.heading: Master skills and projects, not jobs
chunks.text:
The goal was not to stay unemployed. It was to use his 20s to find what he loves and is great at. He started by learning "master skills", which he compares to the one master key on a janitor's ring of 573 keys that opens many doors. His list:
- Making something out of nothing (hustle)
- Selling stuff online (sales/marketing)
- Pitching ideas and getting people on board (persuasion)

He didn't know how to learn these, so he did projects. He borrows Pixar's process: start with something that sucks, then "remove the suck." Every version 1.0 sucks, so you edit and tweak until it no longer does. His job was to make each project, each "dot", as bold as possible and trust they'd connect later (the Steve Jobs line that you can only connect the dots looking backwards).

chunks.heading: The projects and what each taught him
chunks.text:
- **E-commerce store for custom wristbands to frats and sororities:** made $1K in the first weekend. Taught him selling online, finding manufacturers on Alibaba, drop shipping and cold email.
- **Game shows:** he and Dan got cast on Wheel of Fortune and Dan almost won a trip to Italy. Being young gave him "the license to do irrationally dumb things."
- **Video editing for real estate agents:** turned property photos into an animated slideshow video with music for $500, about 15 minutes of editing. Agents were hard to sell to. He learned video editing, more cold email, and that he should favor work where earnings are not tied to his time (unlike tutoring).
- **Poker:** won $10K in a tournament one night and used it to travel Australia. Taught him strategy, thinking in probabilities, controlling his mind and spotting when others are lying.
- **Delivery-only sushi restaurant:** taught him how to make sushi, run a restaurant, negotiate a lease and get bank financing.

None were big financial successes. A few made money and most went nowhere. At the time it felt like striking out repeatedly, but he kept going because it was fun. The skills paid off much later.

chunks.heading: How he decided what to do: Permission to Wander
chunks.text: When asked how he went from sushi, poker and e-commerce to a career, Shaan says he used a 3-step system he calls "Permission to Wander" for figuring out what you want to do in life. This essay only introduces it and defers the steps to a follow-up piece, "the 3-step plan to figuring out what you want."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues that tight constraints unleash creativity rather than limit it. He uses Dr. Seuss's 50-word bet and Spielberg's broken shark in Jaws as examples, then points to his own 'One Minute Blog' format as a self-imposed constraint that outperforms his no-limit posts.

chunks.heading: Constraints as a creative engine
chunks.text:
Shaan argues that creativity thrives under limits, not freedom. His line: "Think outside the box" was wrong. What great creators do is put themselves into a tight box to do their best work.

- Self-discipline unlocks personal freedom (the Goggins/Jocko insight). By the same logic, constraints unleash creativity.
- He backs this with two quotes: "Creativity starts when you cut a zero from your budget" (Jaime Lerner) and "The enemy of art is the absence of limitation" (Orson Welles).

chunks.heading: Dr. Seuss and the 50-word bet
chunks.text:
A case of a constraint deliberately imposed to force a better product.

- In the 1950s Dr. Seuss was on a hot streak with Cat in the Hat and How the Grinch Stole Christmas. Cat in the Hat used only about 236 total words.
- His publisher, Bennett Cerf, upped the ante with a bet: write a children's book using only 50 unique words.
- Seuss won the bet. The result, Green Eggs & Ham, became his best-selling book ever, with 8M+ copies sold.
- Lesson: a tighter limit than his already-minimal style produced his biggest hit.

chunks.heading: Jaws: when the constraint picks you
chunks.text:
Sometimes the limit isn't chosen. Shaan uses Spielberg's Jaws as the example of embracing a forced constraint.

- Attempt 1: use real sharks. The production team said no.
- Attempt 2: build a mechanical shark. It cost $250,000 and broke 3 times because of the water.
- With production nearly paused, Spielberg's reframe was: how do I make a terrifying shark without ever showing it on camera?
- His answers:
  - Triple down on music and lighting.
  - Shoot from the shark's point of view so it's never seen.
  - Show only the shark fin ("a swimmer's nightmare").
- Result: a smash hit, about $500M at the box office on a $7M budget.
- Spielberg later admitted: "If the mechanical sharks had worked, Jaws probably would've been a worse movie."

chunks.heading: The "One Minute Blog" as a self-imposed constraint
chunks.text:
Shaan applies the principle to his own writing.

- His essay series is called the "One Minute Blog." The constraint: write something insightful that takes the reader 1 minute 59 seconds max to read. (This post's read time: 1 min 34 sec.)
- His observation: the "One Minute" posts are far more popular than his no-limit posts.

chunks.heading: How to apply it
chunks.text:
- When facing a blank page or open-ended brief, add a hard cap: word count, time, budget, number of elements.
- When a resource you counted on fails (budget, tool, access), ask what the constraint forces you to do better, rather than how to work around it.
- Treat a tight box as a feature of the work, not a handicap to remove.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues that finding your 'thing' is the only true shortcut in life. Instead of asking what you're great at, notice what everyone else seems mysteriously bad at. He found explaining things after 10 years of being a B+ founder, and his cofounder Ben Levy built a business advantage from staying in touch.

chunks.heading: Finding your thing is the only true shortcut
chunks.text:
Shaan argues that everyone he admires found their "thing," and that finding it is "the only true shortcut to life." He frames it with an analogy: you realize you have a dirt bike, so a little dirt path is perfect for you, even if it won't suit people in cars.

- Michael Phelps: double-jointed elbows, a torso 8 inches too long, and half the lactic acid production of a normal human. "Built like a flying fish," so he found swimming.
- Joe Rogan: liked getting high and having funny conversations with friends about everything from fighting to aliens. Shaan couldn't hold a 3-hour conversation with a stranger, but Joe can, so he found podcasting.
- The point: your thing is what fits your unusual wiring, not what is generally prestigious.

chunks.heading: The question that surfaces it: what is everyone else mysteriously bad at?
chunks.text:
Shaan cites a quote from Ben Kuhn (CTO of Anthropic): "what does it seem like everyone else is mysteriously bad at?"

- He recommends replacing "what am I great at?" with "what does everyone else mysteriously suck at?"
- Reason: most people are too humble, or too self-critical, to admit what they are great at. Noticing what frustrates you about others' incompetence is an easier signal to read.
- Application: pay attention to what seems obvious or easy to you but that others keep getting wrong.

chunks.heading: Shaan's own path: 10 years of "founder," then explaining things
chunks.text:
- He always wondered why other people are so bad at explanations. In school he hated how teachers explained things ("too complicated, too boring"). As an investor he was surprised how bad founders are at telling their own story.
- From age 20 to 30 he tried to make being a great CEO his thing. He "wanted" it to be his thing, but wanting doesn't make it so. He was "a B+ at it. But in the real world, B+ doesn't get you jack sh\*t."
- It took 10 years to find his actual thing. He then started podcasting for fun and writing, which was the thing he thought others were mysteriously bad at: explaining things.
- Results: the podcast hit 100m+ streams, his Twitter grew to 450k followers, and his newsletter grew fast and was sold within 1 year for millions of dollars.
- Lesson: don't force a thing you want to be good at; follow the thing you do naturally and enjoyably, and where you have an edge over others.

chunks.heading: Ben Levy's thing: keeping in touch
chunks.text:
Shaan's cofounder Ben Levy finds it strange that everyone is terrible at keeping in touch. Shaan admits he is guilty of it: he forgets to reply, doesn't check in, and will "have a great lunch meeting, then forget to keep in touch for 2 years."

Ben does the opposite:
- Always replies and loves to check in.
- Texts you if you write a blog post, to say it's great.
- Sends a gift if you have a baby.
- Sends useful links relevant to your project, knows your favorite sports team, and texts after every game.
- Texts about 100 unique people every day, with no agenda, just because he likes it.

Payoff: "We've directly made millions of dollars just because Ben happened to be staying in touch with someone and they thought of us when an opportunity sprang up."

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text:
- Everyone has a thing; you just have to find it, and you may not know it today.
- Your thing is often something you do for fun or without effort that others find hard.
- A "B+" at the thing you wish you were good at loses to being exceptional at the thing you're naturally wired for.
- Habits others see as chores (staying in touch, explaining clearly) can be compounding advantages and a source of deal flow.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues that instead of out-featuring rivals, you can win by deliberately doing less. Using Slate's $25k stripped-down electric truck and Nintendo's low-fi Wii as examples, he shows how counter-positioning turns last place in a crowded market into first place in a new one.

chunks.heading: Underdoing the competition as positioning
chunks.text:
Shaan calls "underdoing the competition" one of his favorite business tactics. Instead of piling on features like everyone else, a company goes the opposite direction and does less.

- His example is the Slate truck, a $25k electric truck with an old-school vibe, which he calls "genius".
- Cars keep getting more complicated: touch screens, butt warmers, and a "Maybe-Gonna-Kill-You" driving mode.
- Slate has no screens and no seat heaters, and it has roll-up windows.
- It is good only for local driving, with a 150 mile battery range.
- At the launch event, Slate said the truck has old-school knobs instead of digital buttons, and "the crowd literally roared."

chunks.heading: All positioning is counter-positioning
chunks.text:
Shaan's rule is: "In marketing: all positioning is counter-positioning." You define yourself by what the rest of the market is not.

- Every other electric car is fancy, expensive and complex.
- Slate is old school, affordable and simple.
- He argues the result is a change of category. Slate would have been last place in the fancy electric car market. Now it is first place in the simple, fun electric truck market.
- The takeaway is to stop competing for rank in a crowded category and pick the opposite attribute of the leaders.

chunks.heading: Be the only, not the best
chunks.text: Shaan backs the idea with Kevin Kelly's line: "Don't aim to be the best, be the only." Underdoing is a way to become the only option in a niche instead of one of many in a crowded field.

chunks.heading: Nintendo Wii as the proof case
chunks.text:
Shaan calls Nintendo the best at this tactic.

- Xbox and Playstation were racing to build the most cutting-edge, high-graphics systems.
- Nintendo shipped a goofy, low-fi Wii at half the price.
- The games were simple enough that "even your mom could play" (Wii Tennis, Bowling).
- The graphics were simple too: cartoon characters rather than ultra-realistic ones.
- It sold over 100M units, outselling both Xbox and Playstation at the time.

chunks.heading: How to apply the underdo tactic
chunks.text:
The steps below are Shaan's pattern as shown in his two examples.

1. Look at the direction your whole market is moving, such as more features, more complexity, higher price or higher fidelity.
2. Go the opposite way: fewer features, a lower price, a simpler product.
3. Accept the limits on purpose, as Slate did with its short range and its local-driving-only focus.
4. Market the simplicity as the headline. The knobs and roll-up windows got a roar from the crowd.
5. Aim to be first place in a new, simpler category rather than last place in the existing one.

He closes with a quote from Ralph Waldo Emerson: "Indeed, to be simple, is to be great."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan's first rule of marketing: nobody cares about your product, they care about themselves. Use the Mario analogy (customer is little Mario, product is the power-up, result is big Mario) and market the outcome the customer gets, not the features.

chunks.heading: Customers want to become big Mario, not hear about the item
chunks.text:
- Shaan's "Rule #1 of marketing": "nobody cares about your product, they care about themselves."
- He frames it with a Mario analogy:
  - Your customer is little Mario: not powerful, needs help.
  - Your product is an item Mario can use.
  - The result is big Mario, shooting fireballs and kicking everyone's ass.
- The marketing job is to sell the big Mario outcome, not the item.

chunks.heading: The common mistake: talking about yourself and your product
chunks.text:
- Shaan says most people "talk endlessly about yourself / your product."
- His alternative: tell customers how awesome they will be after using the product.
- This is the core framework. In his words: "The day you understand this framework, is the day you start learning marketing."

chunks.heading: Why the product is an obstacle, not the draw
chunks.text:
- Shaan stresses, with a "🚨 I REPEAT 🚨", that nobody cares about your product.
- He argues the product is an obstacle for the customer:
  - It has a cost.
  - It takes time to learn.
  - It is "a necessary evil on the way to them getting what they _really want_."
- What people do care about is their own quality of life improving.

chunks.heading: Worked example: breakfast bars
chunks.text:
- Shaan's example applies whatever the business: "If you're selling breakfast bars, don't tell me about the granola."
- Instead of ingredients, lead with outcomes:
  - It saves 20 minutes in the morning by being a grab-and-go breakfast.
  - The buyer loses weight in the process.
- The pattern is to swap product features (granola) for the customer's after-state (time saved, weight lost).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues the AI future is K-shaped: people either get replaced or become 10X more productive by using AI. His fix is to break your job into a bundle of tasks, see which AI can already boost, and learn to manage robots.

chunks.heading: AI will not replace you, but it will split workers into two paths
chunks.text:
- Shaan frames the future of work as "shaped like a K". Two paths diverge from the same starting point.
- Path one: you get replaced by AI. He compares this to being a horse after "Henry Ford just put a car on the road".
- Path two: you learn to use AI and become "10X more productive".
- His point is that the choice is yours. You either learn the tools or get displaced by someone who did.

chunks.heading: Treat your job as a bundle of tasks, not one big thing
chunks.text:
- Shaan's core mental model: stop thinking of your job as one big thing. Think of it as a "bundle of tasks".
- Example, a sales rep's job breaks into:
  - Prospecting potential customers
  - Drafting cold emails
  - Tracking response rates
  - Scheduling calls
  - Doing the calls
  - Writing notes during the call
  - Follow-up emails
  - Drafting proposals
  - Updating the CRM
- The exercise is to list every task in your role, then ask which ones AI can do or boost today.
- Task-level thinking is what lets you see where AI helps instead of reacting to a vague fear of replacement.

chunks.heading: How much of a job AI can do now versus soon
chunks.text:
- Shaan's rough estimate for the 20-task sales rep list: only "2-3 out of 20" tasks can be significantly boosted by AI today.
- He says AI is improving fast and that "soon, half your tasks will be handled by AI".
- Implication: the share of a job that is automatable grows over time, so the bundle you audit now should be re-audited regularly.
- Start with the few tasks AI can already boost, build the habit, and expand as capability grows.

chunks.heading: Managing robots will be worth more than managing humans
chunks.text:
- Shaan's prediction, which he tells readers to "write this down": "in the future being able to 'manage robots' will be more valuable than managing humans."
- His advice is to learn AI tools and get good at directing them, to "make them your baby-back-b\*tch".
- The skill is delegating tasks from your bundle to AI the way a manager delegates to a team, then reviewing and steering the output.
- That ability is what puts you on the upper arm of the K.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues that a few star employees create most of a company's value, yet managers spend most of their time on problem and average employees. He defines stars as people who identify the right problem and then solve it, alone or by coordinating others. He also gives target percentages of "level 5" players by company size.

chunks.heading: The core claim: a company's value comes from its right-side talent
chunks.text:
- Shaan opens with a mentor's line: "everyone sucks in their first 5 years as a manager. It's up to you if you're going to suck for the next 15 too."
- Every company has a distribution of talent, from problem employees on the left, to average employees in the middle, to star employees on the right.
- A manager spends about 90% of their time on the left (problem employees) and the middle (average employees).
- The right side (star employees) creates about 90% of the company's value.
- If you work at a company, he says, be a "right side" player. If you run one, get as many of them as you can.
- He paraphrases Elon's idea in plain terms: "the team you build is the company you build… so build a great team."

chunks.heading: The Triangle of Talent framework
chunks.text:
- He calls it the Triangle of Talent. It "saved my a** many times as a manager."
- Forget job titles: all employees are problem solvers.
- Problem solving has two parts:
  - Identify the right problem to solve.
  - Solve it, either yourself or by coordinating others.
- Star performers live at the top of the triangle.
- He says this makes a simple guide: "That's it. That's the whole game."

chunks.heading: Two questions to test whether someone is a star
chunks.text:
- Are you identifying the A+ problem on a daily, weekly, monthly and annual basis?
- Are you able to solve that problem, either alone or by coordinating other people?
- He applies the same test to himself as a manager and to anyone he is evaluating.

chunks.heading: Picking the problem matters more than solving it
chunks.text:
- He argues most people think the job is about solving the problem, "and it kinda is."
- But the easier and more impactful skill is getting good at figuring out "what problem needs to be solved right now?"
- Practical takeaway: spend effort on choosing the highest-value problem at each time horizon (day, week, month, year) before spending effort on execution.

chunks.heading: How many level 5s a CEO should have
chunks.text:
Level 5 is the top of the triangle (the star performer). His targets by company size:

| Company stage | Target share of level 5s |
|---|---|
| Just started (cofounders) | 100% |
| Small team (5-20 people) | At least 30% |
| Medium team (20-150 people) | Shoot for 15% |
| Big company (150+ people) | 5-10% |

- On big companies he adds: "honestly just quit, big companies are no fun."
- The framing for CEOs: count your level 5s and compare against the target for your size.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan, who has built 500k+ email subscribers, 400k+ Twitter followers, 500k+ YouTube subscribers and 100M+ podcast downloads, shares nine lessons for building an audience. Core ideas: optimize for who follows you, not how many; make content about your inner nerd; build a magnet and a "binge bank"; sell a feeling; and get good through reps.

chunks.heading: Quality beats follower count
chunks.text:
- Shaan says to focus on WHO follows him, not HOW MANY follow him. He tries to ignore the numbers, because platforms shove them in your face (on YouTube everyone else can see them too).
- Ignoring view counts and prioritizing quality is a competitive advantage, since most people fall into the numbers trap.
- He cites Tim Ferriss: "Would you rather 100,000 Americans, chosen at random, read your book? Or be invisible to them - but every attendee of Davos loves your work?" He picks the latter.
- Car analogy: General Motors sells 2.6M cars a year and is worth $50B. Ferrari sells 13,000 cars and is worth $80B. Ferrari has 200x fewer customers yet is more valuable, because each customer is worth 200+ of a competitor's.
- Applied to content: if Elon Musk loves his blog, that one reader is worth more than 100,000 TikTok views from random viewers.
- Rule: "Quality matters more than quantity."

chunks.heading: Find your inner nerd to decide what to talk about
chunks.text:
- He quotes his trainer: "the best product is just you, pushed out to the world." He calls this finding your inner nerd.
- Ask what you nerd out about most: the topic that looks boring or like work to others but feels like play to you, and that you have an unquenchable thirst for.
- Example: his uncle's basement model train set. Shaan thought he was a dork, but says that for content he wants to be the basement model train guy, doing it publicly for the world.
- Example creator: the "die, workwear!" guy, who writes 1,000-word analyses of what pant length men should wear on suits, and enjoys it.
- Two benefits:
  - It eliminates competition, since very few people share your taste palette.
  - It makes success a guarantee. If success only means "am I famous with millions of followers yet?", you may be unhappy forever. If you nerd out and have fun daily, every day is a win. He says this shifts the odds of success "from 1% to 100% because I win by playing (vs. only winning by winning)."

chunks.heading: Build a magnet, not an audience
chunks.text:
- He thinks of content as a giant magnet that attracts the type of people he wants in his life.
- Every blog, podcast and video should be a honeypot for like-minded people.
- "The internet is a geography vaporizer." He loves old Berkshire Hathaway meetings, basketball and building startups, and nobody in the neighborhood he grew up in likes those things. The internet lets him find the 10,000 people who share his flavor of weird.
- His goal: "build a magnet, not an audience."

chunks.heading: The 5 D's: be known well, not well known
chunks.text:
- His goal is not to be well known but to be "known well", which means sharing stories, hopes, dreams, fears and obsessions.
- The 5 D's:
  - Done: what you've done, your track record.
  - Deliver: what you offer people who follow you.
  - Do: what you do for work and for fun.
  - Dreams: what you're shooting for (e.g. Gary V wants to buy the Jets).
  - Dork Out: what you're really into, what you collect.
- Two wins:
  - The audience feels more connection.
  - You get luckier, because fans know what to send you: links (obscure stories of rich people), book recommendations (he's studying comedy and storytelling), and deals ($1m+ annual cash flow, bootstrapped, needing growth help).
- He also argues there's no such thing as too long, only "too boring."

chunks.heading: Prioritize content over packaging; build a binge bank
chunks.text:
- "A+ content with C- delivery is a great starting point. C- content with A+ delivery is a death trap."
- He didn't waste hours on packaging. He spent years living an interesting life so he had something interesting to say.
- Example: Joe Rogan's first podcast episode had an ugly webcam, snowflake video effects and a rainbow background. Rogan focused on content first and packaging later, and is now the king of podcasts.
- Binge bank: when numbers were small and he doubted the point, he told himself he was building a binge bank, "a personal Netflix binge-worthy show", about 1 hour of content that, if someone consumed it, would make them love him.
- The trick is to picture future people discovering his content, clicking to learn more, and falling into the binge bank, instead of thinking about the 8 people viewing today.

chunks.heading: Sell a feeling, not information
chunks.text:
- He thinks of his channel as a little shop at the world's most crowded flea market, and says he's not selling things but a feeling.
- Examples of feelings sold:
  - David Blaine: awe.
  - James Clear: self-control.
  - UFC: "holy shit!" moments, live on PPV.
  - Tony Robbins: motivation.
  - CrossFit: a satisfying sweat.
- Give the feeling once or twice and you get a follow. Give it every day and you get a lifelong fan.
- His method: figure out which feeling he wants to sell, then deliver it consistently.

chunks.heading: Be so good they can't ignore you (MrBeast's advice)
chunks.text:
- Shaan, a friend of MrBeast's, shares his advice for aspiring YouTubers: "Make 100 videos, and every video, try to do one thing better. Maybe it's the hook. Or the thumbnail. Or storytelling. Whatever. Just make one thing better, every time, then come back and talk to me after 100."
- Why it works:
  - It shoos away unserious people, since almost nobody takes the advice.
  - Those who do take it have figured it out themselves by video 100.
- On blaming the algorithm, MrBeast says to replace "algorithm" with "people": not "the algorithm doesn't like my video" but "people don't like my video."
- Shaan's takeaway: the algorithm serves people videos they like to watch, so failure is "a skill issue."
- Content is a skill, a muscle developed through reps. The strategy: "become so good they can't ignore you."

chunks.heading: Credentials behind the lessons
chunks.text:
- Over the past 5 years he built audiences of 500k+ email subscribers, 400k+ Twitter followers, 500k+ YouTube subscribers, and 100,000,000+ total downloads of his podcast.
- He did this for himself, his company and his podcast.
- He skips obvious advice like "be consistent" and shares 9 non-obvious lessons.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues balance is the wrong goal because it turns life into a zero-sum rationing game. His alternative is integration: stack goals into single activities and pick work that pays for results, feels like play, and leaves you control of your schedule.

chunks.heading: Life balance is the wrong goal; integration is the right one
chunks.text:
- Shaan says "there is no such thing as 'Life Balance'", and that it's not even the right goal. He treats "balance" as polite code for "I want everything".
- Most people have about 5 top priorities and a fixed budget of "life points" (energy, time, money, attention). Balance-seekers ration them.
- Rationing gives every area roughly 50% effort, so nothing hits 0% and nothing hits 100%. He calls this "a recipe for mediocrity & disappointment" and a zero-sum game of constant trade-offs between work, family, fitness, friends and fun.

chunks.heading: Three doors: balance, zero expectations, integration
chunks.text:
- **Door 1, "Balance":** living with an expectation of balance. He says Reality - Expectation = Unhappiness. These people feel like they're doing something wrong, or blame the boss, the government or the system.
- **Door 2, "Zero expectations":** blast your life points at whatever matters right now. Typically fun and work in your 20s, family and work in your 30s, travel and health in your 60s. Still zero-sum, but happier.
- **Door 3, "Integration":** what Shaan says the "winners of life" do. They have the money, body, family, fun and peace of mind, and you rarely hear from them because they're too busy living.
- The core idea: instead of choosing between two buckets, make one activity fill several. "Integration multiplies your time." About 16 waking hours a day, but one hour filling 3 life buckets multiplies it.

chunks.heading: Shaan's own integrations
chunks.text:
- **Health + friends:** works out with his buddy John every morning and plays basketball with friends once a week. When people ask for a coffee meeting, he proposes a hike, walk or workout instead. He says the shared struggle builds relationships faster.
- **Friends + work:** most of his friends are entrepreneurs, so hanging out yields marketing, operations and investment ideas.
- **Wife + work:** he started a business with his wife and they built a ~$25M company together. Caveats: it only works because she is a strong business partner, and they learned to "turn it off" so they stay life partners, not just business partners. He warns it "can be disastrous if done wrong".
- **Fun + health:** a weekly basketball league and workouts with buddies make exercise a fun part of the day instead of solo gym grinding.

chunks.heading: Work is the biggest bucket, so fix work first
chunks.text:
- Most people spend 8 hours a day at work. If work isn't fun, isn't done with people you like, and doesn't give you schedule freedom, integration is very hard.
- His analogy: a power outlet with no holes, so nothing else can plug in. After his career change he's "a power strip", "swiss cheese", "putt putt golf" with holes everywhere.

chunks.heading: The "time test" for jobs
chunks.text:
- Test: if you worked for one hour, closed your laptop and left, having done as much as a co-worker who sat there 8 hours, would your boss be mad at you or at the co-worker?
- He says in 99% of jobs the boss would be mad at you, even though they claim to be "results driven". That means you're paid for time, not results.
- Shaan held a job for 1 year and disliked it for this reason.

chunks.heading: How Shaan restructured his career
chunks.text:
- He then spent 8 years as an entrepreneur, mostly failing, but kept going because: he enjoyed it (never knew what day of the week it was, a green flag), his friends were his coworkers, and a big hit meant lasting financial freedom.
- Two people made him jealous, "like they had cheat codes for life":
  - **An investor** who gets paid to have lunch with smart people and picks about 1 in 20 to give money to. He notes most funds use a 2/20 model: 2% of the fund per year in fees (on a $50M fund, $1M a year for 10 years) plus 20% of profits.
  - **Tim Ferriss**, whose fireside chat drew nearly 1,000 ticket buyers to hear one person talk in a chair, with no music or pyrotechnics.
- After selling his company he skipped starting another one and told people he was now a podcaster and investor, with no podcasting skills and a small investing bankroll. He turned down every job offer and term sheet to start a new company.
- Four years later: his podcast My First Million is mostly calling his friend Sam and talking business for an hour. Halfway through he reads a Hubspot CRM ad. He gets paid more than he ever imagined for something he'd do for free. As an investor, founders call him, do the hard work, and he takes a piece of the upside.

chunks.heading: Checklist for finding your "thing"
chunks.text:
Find work that:

- You'd do as a hobby and can't believe you get paid for.
- Pays for results, not time-in-chair.
- Has top performers earning 10x or 100x the average (he says this is almost every field: plumbers, chefs, doctors).
- Gives you control over your schedule.

His conclusion: "If you find that, then you can do integration, and never need balance." Examples of "work that feels like play" he gives: writing books (Ryan Holiday), teaching people to code, owning a gym.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues the single most important trait in a partner is being "down": quick to commit, willing to do whatever the mission needs, and biased toward immediate action. He illustrates with his partner Ben, Greg Brockman at OpenAI, Airbnb and Uber, and explains why down partners enable pivots and high-upside bets.

chunks.heading: Why "down" is the one trait Shaan looks for in a partner
chunks.text:
- Shaan says the most important trait in a business partner (and a life partner) is being "down". He compresses this from Warren Buffett's three criteria (intelligence, integrity, energy), which he used to follow.
- He frames partner choice as the highest-stakes decision: a median marriage (age 30 to 76) is 46 uninterrupted years (16,790 days), and divorce costs about 50% of net worth in a day. A business partnership has no structured "divorce" and unwinding it is messy.
- He grants that other traits matter (intelligence, unselfishness, energy, integrity), but says "the most important trait for me is how down they are."

chunks.heading: The three meanings of "down"
chunks.text:
- "Down for whatever": flexible. You can throw any plan or idea at them and they roll with the punches.
- "Down for the cause": puts the team and mission ahead of their own needs.
- "Down to do it": an action word, not a personality trait like "smart". Down people act now. They don't wait, don't overthink, they start and figure it out.
- Their filters for action are simple: Does this sound interesting? Do I like this person? Can I be useful here? Does anything smell fishy? If fine, "OK, I'm down."

chunks.heading: Ben as the example of a great partner
chunks.text:
- Shaan has worked with his business partner Ben for nearly 5 years and wants to do 20 more. They have built and sold companies together, done side projects and traveled.
- Ben is "smart, but not the smartest" and has a good work ethic but isn't "David Goggins". What defines him is that he is down: for the cause, to try it, to start right now.
- Ben was a 25-year-old mid-level employee at FanDuel, not a coder or a sales star. When a FanDuel founder wanted to leave and start a new company, he picked Ben because he was down.
- When Shaan met Ben, Ben had a SaaS business making about $1M a year in profit but was bored. Shaan pitched a half-baked side project that would initially pay him less. Ben decided on the spot: "yea, I'm down."
- Shaan asked if he needed to sleep on it. Ben replied he hadn't been listening because he had already gone to GoDaddy to buy the domain and set up the site that night. Shaan's takeaway: being down gives you an incredible bias for action.

chunks.heading: Other examples of down partners
chunks.text:
- Greg Brockman and OpenAI: Shaan cites Sam Altman's essay about Greg. He commits quickly and fully. After Sam pitched him on OpenAI, he asked questions for the first 30 minutes of the drive to San Francisco, declared "I'm in" halfway, and spent the last 30 minutes starting the job. He was a brilliant coder (former CTO of Stripe) but also took on non-technical grunt work like getting meals, cleaning up and ordering supplies.
- Airbnb: Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia weren't coders or growth hackers, but when they needed cash, Brian floated turning their apartment into an "air bed and breakfast". You need a partner down enough to float an idea like that, let alone pull it off.
- Uber: when Travis and Garrett needed someone to run a weird black car, off-market taxi service, Ryan Graves answered their tweet. He had a modest background, wasn't a tech genius or polished CEO, but was ready to start yesterday.

chunks.heading: Why speed of commitment beats overthinking
chunks.text:
- Shaan compares it to two people jumping from one cliff to another: it's not about who has stronger quads, but who can mentally commit to the jump.
- Even if a down person misses something 1 time out of 10, they move 10x faster than over-thinkers and get 10x more shots on goal.
- Being down drives action and reduces fear, doubt and judgment.

chunks.heading: Why a partner who isn't down kills high-upside ideas
chunks.text:
- New ideas are uncertain and the odds look slim. A partner who flinches at uncertainty is contagious and pulls you toward conservative, safe, proven paths, where there is very little upside.
- The damage is unspoken. Like having a very conservative friend, you pre-filter what you'll bring them. With a non-down partner, you filter out high-upside paths before they ever see daylight.
- You need a partner who is down for off-the-beaten-path ideas.

chunks.heading: Pivots require a down partner
chunks.text:
- Nearly every great business pivots at least once. Examples he gives: Instagram started as a location app, Slack was a multiplayer game, Twitter was a podcasting app.
- Product, market, price point and marketing strategy are "a giant guess up front". Pivoting means saying on day 458 "we were wrong, everything we've said the past year and a half is wrong... the name is changing, the plan is changing."
- You can only pull off that mid-air U-turn if your partner is down. "Weak stomachs can't handle the sudden shifts."

chunks.heading: How to spot down people and when it matters
chunks.text:
