- Shaan uses the Reticular Activating System as an analogy: just as you can't name 5 red things in your room until you look for them, then find them easily, once you look for down people you'll spot them.
- You can get away with 90% of life with someone who isn't down, because most things are safe, predictable and figured out.
- For life's great adventures (traveling, starting businesses, making art, having kids), which require daily leaps of faith, he says to pick someone who is down.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan retells 22 events that pushed Elon into backing Trump and extracts his operating pattern: find the existential problem, pick the key lever, burn the boats. Also covers risk as game theory, +EV bets with outsized upside, and separating credibility from likeability.

chunks.heading: Elon's decision framework: the "Elon Method"
chunks.text:
Shaan distills how Elon makes high-stakes bets into three steps:

1. Figure out the most existential problem.
2. Identify the key lever (e.g. Pennsylvania as the swing state).
3. Go all in. "Burn all boats. Throw your entire weight at it."

His one-liner: "If you play - play to win." He frames Elon's 2024 election push as a game-theory choice. Doing nothing risks losing, doing a little may not matter, and going all in can tilt a 50/50 race. Elon "doesn't process risk the same way the rest of us" do. Most people look at a coin flip and call all-in "too risky."

chunks.heading: Why Elon went all in on Trump: the +EV math
chunks.text:
Shaan treats the $150M election spend as an expected-value bet, not a gamble:

- Elon spent about $150M out of pocket (about $1M per day, plus moving to Pennsylvania, speeches, X town halls, and getting Trump on Joe Rogan).
- His companies are worth about $1 trillion.
- If the move gives them even a 1% goodwill boost, that is about $10B in gains, or "$150M to get $10B." Shaan calls it "a +EV decision."
- Upside he lists: a pro-tech, pro-crypto, pro-business, anti-regulation government, a giant "I-owe-you" from Trump, and "the tears of his enemies."
- Downside Shaan acknowledges: the polls were tight, and a loss would have made Elon "screwed" with Democrats who already disliked him.

chunks.heading: The 22-event backstory: pressure that pushed Elon into politics
chunks.text:
Shaan's narrative of how Elon went from apolitical engineer to campaign volunteer:

- 2020: Elon is "not political," just wants to build cars, rockets, and tunnels.
- A California congresswoman tweets "F*ck Elon Musk." He replies "message received" and moves his companies to Texas.
- Biden holds an EV summit and invites every car maker except Tesla. Shaan's explanation: unions back the Democrats, and Tesla is the only major non-unionized car maker.
- Twitter bans the sitting President. Elon sees free speech at risk and buys Twitter for $44B.
- He releases the "Twitter Files." Shaan says they showed Democrats trying to censor social media during the election.
- Government lawsuits and over-regulation of his companies follow. Advertisers boycott Twitter, revenue drops 80%, and Shaan puts the asset's value loss at $20B. Elon fires 80% of staff.
- A holder of 9 Tesla shares sues, and a judge revokes Elon's $56B Tesla pay package. Shaan notes the package was already earned, the metrics were hit, and the stock was up 10X.
- Shaan's read: Elon was "backed into a corner," so he went all in on Trump for three months.

chunks.heading: Credibility is not likeability
chunks.text:
Shaan flags his own bias, 1,100 words of "30 different flavors of 'omg, i love Elon'," then states a principle: "I just don't mix up credibility with likeability."

- He doesn't like Elon's jokes or all his opinions.
- He still calls him "undeniably the greatest entrepreneur of our lifetime."
- The takeaway: learn from people's results and methods without needing to agree with or like them.

chunks.heading: Why Elon's work stands out: "the hardest hardware"
chunks.text:
Shaan notes the Silicon Valley saying "Hardware is Hard" and lists what Elon works on:

- Self-driving electric cars
- Reusable rockets
- Tunnels
- AGI
- Chips in brains

His contrast: "Normal founders celebrate app launches. This guy launches rockets and catches them on lily pads in the ocean like it's a YouTube trick shot video."

chunks.heading: xAI: responding to a loss by going all in on speed
chunks.text:
Shaan's "single favorite Elon story":

- Elon co-founded OpenAI and gave it $40M of his own money, yet ended up with zero ownership and zero say.
- Instead of "taking an L," he created xAI, despite a big disadvantage: OpenAI had a 10-year head start and $10B+ in Microsoft funding.
- His response was to go all in, building the biggest GPU supercluster in the world in 19 days.
- Shaan points to Jensen Huang (NVIDIA CEO) talking about it as proof of how unusual that speed is.

chunks.heading: Change the game instead of playing the opponent's
chunks.text:
Shaan closes with a chess analogy from a new xAI hire that he says sums up Elon's last four years: "it doesn't matter if you're mate in 3...If there's a laser beam from space that shoots down your opponent's king, you win."

- When behind, Elon doesn't try to out-play the leader on the same board.
- He changes the rules with a bigger, faster, more extreme move, using the same all-in approach as the election and xAI.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues every reason we give ourselves is really an excuse we choose to believe, and that excuses can push us toward action or away from it. Using a trainer, Hormozi's hero/villain line and Mike Posner's rattlesnake story, he says setbacks can be reasons to quit or to restart.

chunks.heading: Excuses are neutral: pick ones that move you forward
chunks.text:
Shaan's core claim: "Life changes once you realize everything is an excuse." An excuse is "simply a reason that you make up and choose to believe in," and it can be positive or negative. The things we call reasons are all just excuses, so you get to decide which ones to hold.

- He asks: "Are you going to find excuses to feel shitty, and be shitty? Or find excuses to feel good, and do good?"
- The shift is from treating circumstances as causes to treating them as stories you pick.
- Applied to work and discipline, it means choosing the interpretation that gets you to act.

chunks.heading: Same circumstance, opposite excuse: the tired-workout example
chunks.text:
Shaan gives a simple example of one fact producing two opposite decisions.

- Shaan wakes up tired and takes it as a great excuse to skip his workout: "I'm tired! Surely I need rest."
- His trainer wakes up tired and reasons the opposite: he needs a quick workout to get his body moving so he doesn't feel sluggish.
- The trainer "found an excuse _to do it_." Shaan "found an excuse to _not do it._"
- Lesson: the condition (tiredness) doesn't decide the behavior. The story you attach to it does.

chunks.heading: Pain as fuel: heroes and villains share the same back story
chunks.text:
Shaan cites Alex Hormozi's line on pain as something you can use or be used by:

"Heroes and villains always have the same back story, pain. The difference is what they choose to do about it. Villain says 'the world hurt me, I'll hurt it back.' Hero says 'the world hurt me, I'm not gonna let it hurt anyone else. Heroes use pain. Villains are used by it.'"

- He endorses this as the frame for choosing a positive excuse.
- The same setback can justify quitting, bitterness or harm, or justify building something and helping others.

chunks.heading: Mike Posner's walk across America: an excuse to restart
chunks.text:
Shaan tells the story from a podcast he did with Mike Posner (writer of "I Took A Pill In Ibiza").

- After his friend Avicii died, Mike used the sadness as an excuse to do something on his bucket list, because life is short: walk across America.
- He covered about two-thirds of the way, was bitten by a rattlesnake and nearly died. He was hospitalized, doctors said he might lose the leg, and he spent a few weeks re-learning how to walk.
- Once he could walk again, he went straight back to the spot where the snake bit him and resumed.
- Nobody would have faulted him for stopping. Mike's framing: "everyone expected me to quit. Either this is an excuse to stop. Or it's an excuse to restart. So I went back and restarted. And when I did that, I became someone new."
- Takeaway Shaan draws: the same near-death event can be a reason to stop or a reason to restart, and the person chooses which.

chunks.heading: How to use the idea
chunks.text:
- When you catch yourself with a reason not to do something (tired, hurt, setback), recognize it as an excuse you are choosing, not a fact that forces your hand.
- Look for the opposite excuse that pushes you toward action, as the trainer did with tiredness and Mike did with the snakebite.
- Treat painful events as material to use rather than something that uses you.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan uses a Weight Watchers stock call (down 90%+, then up 166% in a month) to introduce "mispriced assets": things that are overlooked or misunderstood. He applies the lens to personality traits, arguing showmanship and playfulness are undervalued, and illustrates it with a basketball-coach prank.

chunks.heading: Mispriced assets: look for what's overlooked or misunderstood
chunks.text:
- Shaan's frame: "mispriced assets" are "things that are overlooked, or misunderstood." Stocks are one place to find them, but he looks for them in daily life too.
- Example: Weight Watchers stock. It was down 90%+, with a market cap of only $60M, for a company "that everyone and their mom has heard of."
- His read: weight loss didn't go away and wasn't a fad, since "we're still fatter than ever." Ozempic (and other factors) had crushed the stock.
- On the podcast he said it "looks mispriced" and that he'd buy some stock that day. A month later the stock was up +166%.
- He doesn't claim to be a stock-picking genius. The point is the habit of spotting assets the market has written off for the wrong reasons.

chunks.heading: Personality traits can be mispriced too
chunks.text:
- Shaan asks which personality traits are undervalued.
- Being smart is fairly priced: "Everyone wants to be smart."
- His pick for an undervalued trait is showmanship. As people become "bent-neck nerds, staring at phones," old-school showmanship has become rare, which makes it scarcer and more valuable.

chunks.heading: Story: the free throw that made a coach's year
chunks.text:
- Shaan, a 36-year-old out-of-shape tech guy, hired a basketball skills coach. His reason: running on a treadmill is miserable, and playing basketball makes him happy.
- The coach normally trains NBA prospects. Shaan showed up with greying hair, mismatched socks and a Michael Scott-style tank-top jersey.
- The coach asked for a free throw to see his form and baseline. Shaan dribbled, exhaled and threw up an intentionally ugly shot (a CLANK).
- After the coach's stunned reaction, Shaan paused, said "I'm just kidding man," shot a normal free throw and made it.
- The coach laughed and said it was his favorite moment at work all year. He told his coworkers and was still laughing about it at the next session.
- Shaan's takeaway: about 10 seconds of playfulness made someone's day and created a memorable impression.

chunks.heading: Don't let the world beat the playfulness out of you
chunks.text:
- Adults tend to lose their playfulness and showmanship because "the world wants you to be serious."
- Shaan questions that: "Why so serious? Everybody likes fun." He thinks people treat fun as "wrong or inappropriate" when it isn't.
- His daily action: find a moment to play, and do something with "a little finesse. A little style. A little…showmanship!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues the most important voice in your life is your inner monologue, which acts as director of your life's movie. Events are neutral; the meaning you attach is a choice, so when the voice spews negativity (like after launching his podcast), ask it for other stories and pick the one that serves you.

chunks.heading: The voice in your head is the real power broker
chunks.text:
- Shaan opens with a question: who is the most important voice in your life? He rules out parents (huge influence for 18 years, then time with them drops suddenly), teachers (a few good ones, but not the most important), and friends (influential, since groups end up talking, dressing and aiming alike).
- His answer is "None of the above": "The most important voice in your life is the one that no one else hears." That voice is the director of your life's movie. It tells you what to say, where to stand, when to shut up, and what the story means.
- He cites studies that humans have up to ~60k thoughts per day, ~80% of which skew negative and ~95% of which are repetitive. These are "factory settings", and like a good toy you can change them to be what you want.

chunks.heading: Source idea: Jim Loehr's "power broker"
chunks.text:
- Shaan credits the concept to Tim Ferriss, who told him he read *Mental Toughness Training For Sports* by Dr. Jim Loehr in a bunk bed at 17 and it changed his life.
- The book's core line, as Shaan quotes it: "The power broker in your life is the voice that no one ever hears. It is the master storyteller, and the stories we tell ourselves are our reality."
- Shaan's takeaway: the stories we tell ourselves are our reality.

chunks.heading: Shaan's podcast launch example
chunks.text:
- When he launched his podcast he **hoped** it would be a hit. He pushed publish and waited. Nothing happened: no texts, no tweets, not even a bad review. "Nothing, nada, zilch."
- He then played the first minute himself, and his inner voice said: "Ew. Is that what I sound like? Why am I saying 'like' so many times? This sucks. I hope nobody hears this."
- His point: the voice can give you two opposite messages about any new thing you try, a discouraging one or an encouraging one. Same event, different story.

chunks.heading: Which story is true: whichever one you believe
chunks.text:
- He argues the story you believe is the one that becomes true for you.
- Smarter people resist this because they think there is an objective "truth". He counters with Elon's line: "Physics is the law. Everything else is a suggestion."
- Everything in your life is neutral. "It's the meaning we put ON it that gives it a positive or negative spin."

chunks.heading: The practice: ask the voice for other stories
chunks.text:
1. Notice the voice when it starts narrating.
2. Pause and ask it to produce alternative stories: what else is on the menu, what else could be true?
3. Pick the story that serves you.

- He closes with Garry Tan's line from MFM: "the key to life is realizing that it's all made up… but you get to make it up."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan answers a reader stuck in a "good but not great" life with one word: move. He explains how he left a cushy job in Australia for San Francisco, where the surrounding culture reset his ambition, and argues you should relocate to wherever your people are densest.

chunks.heading: Move to where the best soil is
chunks.text:
- Shaan's one-word answer to a 27-year-old with a "good but not great" life in Nashville is "move". He says the easiest self-improvement lever is often changing your surroundings: "If you want flowers to bloom, plant your seeds in great soil."
- His own case: at 23 he was in Australia making a very cushy $120k/year with an easy job in a beautiful city. He quit and moved to San Francisco with no job and no contacts, because that is the best soil for startups.
- His conclusion: "proximity is power."

chunks.heading: Cities set the status game
chunks.text:
- On his first day in SF he sat in a coffee shop next to a founder pitching a VC. The VC took 30-minute pitch meetings all day, and Shaan eavesdropped for 4 hours. He thought the ideas were terrible ("Uber for masseuses!").
- At a founder meetup that night, almost everyone had a "billion dollar idea". The exception was Craig, who worked at Deloitte and apologized and made excuses for it when introducing himself.
- His takeaway: SF is the only city where startups are normal and jobs are weird. "The high-status thing was low-status here. That's a powerful motivator."
- He cites Paul Graham: "every city whispers something in your ear."
  - LA whispers "you're not beautiful enough"
  - NYC whispers "you're not rich enough"
  - SF whispers "you're not ambitious enough"
- He says the whisper isn't always healthy, but it's always motivating. This is why actors move to Hollywood and startups move to SF.

chunks.heading: What moving does and how to pick where
chunks.text:
- Moving shakes up your routine, social circle, pace, thinking and lifestyle, and forces you to re-think your routines.
- Where to move: "Go where your nerds are." Whatever you are nerdy about, find the place with the highest density of like-minded nerds.
- Example: to build muscle, live in a house with a bunch of gym bros. Soon you will have a gym routine, drink pre-workouts and guzzle protein.
- He frames a comfortable life as fine if that's what you want, but advises moving if you feel you are wasting your potential.

chunks.heading: Hiring talent beyond your location
chunks.text: - For people who ignore advice from internet bros, he suggests hiring talent as far away as possible, and points to Somewhere.com for getting top overseas talent. This is a sponsor plug in the newsletter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan retells Mohnish Pabrai's story of building a $100M+ fortune through "shamelessly cloning", using Tom Peters' parable of two gas stations. Most people watch a competitor win and still don't change their behavior, so deliberately becoming a great copier of great ideas is an edge. Copy the idea and add your own twist, not the exact art.

chunks.heading: Copy great ideas shamelessly
chunks.text:
Shaan's core claim, via Mohnish Pabrai (the "Indian Warren Buffett," $100M+ fortune): his whole strategy was "Two words… Shamelessly Cloning." Shaan loves the phrase and treats it as a working principle for building.

- Mohnish read a Tom Peters book (Peters was a big 1980s management guru) arguing that humans are surprisingly bad at copying successful ideas.
- He made a promise to himself to become "a great copier of great ideas."
- Shaan's takeaway: you may not be the smart operator who figures everything out, but you can choose not to be the one who ignores what is visibly working.

chunks.heading: The story of two gas stations
chunks.text:
Shaan retells Peters' example. Two gas stations with snacks sit across the street from each other, with the same concept.

- **Owner A** pays a guy $150 to improve his signage and installs brighter evening lights. His traffic goes up a bit. He also walks outside to give regular customers a complimentary window wash. He keeps making small service improvements and eventually earns 2-3x more per week than the station across the street.
- **Owner B** calls the signage "a waste of money" and calls the window wash unsustainable ("you can't do it for everyone. And they're not even paying for it!"). He never changes.
- The interesting question, per Shaan, is not what the smart owner does but "why the heck is owner B not doing what he sees is working??" He asks whether it is ego or ignorance.

chunks.heading: Competitors won't act even if you tell them everything
chunks.text:
Shaan relays Peters' argument that this behavior is common and that information alone does not change behavior.

- You can go to direct competitors and tell them all your trade secrets and everything you have learned.
- They will listen, but there will be "no change in behavior."
- Implication: the edge of copying is rarely about access to information. It is about willingness to act on what you can already see.

chunks.heading: The right way to copy: take the idea, not the art
chunks.text:
Shaan cites Picasso: "Good artists borrow. Great artists steal." He is explicit that there is a bad way to copy.

- Don't copy people's art or the exact execution.
- In the gas station case, don't copy the exact signage. Copy the idea ("I should make my business look more approachable too") and put your own twist on it.
- The unit to clone is the underlying insight, then adapt it.

chunks.heading: Copying is often positive-sum
chunks.text:
Shaan gives examples where copying is encouraged by the source and benefits everyone:

- Religion is people copying the morals and beliefs of others, and religions want you to copy them.
- CrossFit is people copying the exercise habits of fit people.
- Grandma's spaghetti recipe is a copy of someone else's spaghetti recipe.

chunks.heading: Shaan's own practice and a hiring tactic
chunks.text:
- He keeps a list of great ideas he plans to "shamelessly clone" and shares it with readers.
- He recommends hiring top 1% talent from South America at $7-10 per hour for "MBA level talent."
- He offers intros to his contact for this: email one line describing the talent needed (e.g. "I need an EA").

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues that "later" and "someday" are the most dangerous words for ambition, because things never settle down and you just stay busy. He urges acting on your dreams now, especially in your 20s "Ramen Era" when you have maximum flexibility and nothing to lose.

chunks.heading: "Someday" and "later" kill dreams: do it now
chunks.text:
- Shaan's core claim is that the "safe path" is not actually safe. It is "dangerous to your dreams."
- He frames safety as a slow killer: "Safety murders your ambition. Murders your sense of adventure. Safety is a serial killer. But it operates in a slow, boring fashion."
- The usual script is "first, let's settle down, take the job, play it safe," on the assumption that you can "always do that later."
- Examples of dreams that get postponed: traveling the world, falling in love, starting a company, a trip to Europe "until things settle down."

chunks.heading: Why "later" never comes
chunks.text:
- "Things never settle down. You simply stay busy. And 'later' never comes."
- He calls "later" "one of the most dangerous words in the english language." When he hears it, he puts his "dukes up ready to fight."
- "Later" and "Someday" have "murdered more dreams than you can count."
- The safe path also keeps people stuck in an "OK" relationship or in the city they grew up in.
- People become "pavlovian dogs," trained to stay put in what they're already doing. They lose the muscle to go chase what they actually want.
- This is why, he says, "youth is wasted on the young."

chunks.heading: The Ramen Era vs. the Mortgage Era
chunks.text:
- Ages 20-27 are "the Ramen Era": a golden window where you don't mind sleeping on the couch, can live off ramen and free refills, and have nobody to take care of but yourself.
- You may be broke and unskilled, but you have "maximum flexibility and nothing to lose."
- Life swings between the Ramen Era and the Mortgage Era, which he illustrates with a chart.
- On the value of youth: "Warren Buffett would give every dollar he has, just to trade places with the average 22 year old dipshit who spent the last year doing beer runs for Sigma Chi."
- Young people get seduced by "Someday" and "Later," which whisper that there is plenty of time to do the real thing after the current thing.

chunks.heading: What to do instead
chunks.text:
- Start the business, tour with the band, backpack through Thailand, whatever it is: "Do it. And do it now."
- Don't wait until you're 31 with "a wife and kids and a mortgage." His line: "You gotta risk it for the biscuit."
- If you're 31, now is still the right time. It beats waiting until 41, "with an achy back," as someone who hasn't taken risks for 20 years.
- Rule of thumb: "If you're called to do something, the only right time is right now."
- Go on adventures and quests. "Find the people you love, and the projects you were put on earth to do."
- Resist "the illusion of safety."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues hard work alone doesn't equal success. The real leverage is finding a business that is a natural extension of who you are, so it feels like play to you and looks like work to others, then becoming the best at it so the internet finds and rewards you.

chunks.heading: "Hard work" is not the key to success
chunks.text:
- Shaan rejects "hard work is the key to success" as incomplete. His test: if hard work determined pay, construction workers sweating all day would out-earn the architect who drew the house or the banker who pushed a button to approve the construction loan.
- He argues that wealthy people like to credit "hard work" because it sounds fairer than the truth. He jokes the honest version is "I'm just smarter than you, and my father paid for private math tutoring while you were stuck picking boogers in daycare."
- His position: "Hard work helps. Certainly. But hard work alone doesn't equal success."
- He mocks the endless list of "keys to success" on Instagram and Pinterest ("passion", "hard work", "discipline", "determination"): "how many god damn keys are there? I need a janitor's keychain."

chunks.heading: "Find the product that is you pushed out"
chunks.text:
- The best career advice Shaan says he got came from his personal trainer, when he asked what to do next in his career: "Find the product that is you pushed out."
- His definition: find a thing so natural to you that doing it is just an extension of being yourself.
- His own example is his podcast. He and his friend Sam already loved nerding out about business and making dumb jokes, and did it for fun with no microphone. Adding a microphone turned it into a job.
- His reaction: "Hard work? This feels like play. I can't believe my luck. I get paid to do this?!"
- The key idea, which he frames with a Naval quote: the work "looks like work to others" but feels like play to you.

chunks.heading: Examples of work that looks hard but feels like play
chunks.text:
- **His personal trainer:** does 5-6 workouts a day with clients, which looks exhausting to Shaan. The trainer loves it and is full of energy. That energy makes him a magnet for clients, and he has a waiting list.
- **Nick Gray:** a social butterfly who loved it enough to write a book, "The 2 Hour Cocktail Party", on hosting gatherings. He now gets paid $10K+ to fly to parties or events and host them.
- **Joe Rogan:** broke the usual podcasting rules. Three-hour interviews ("too long!"), no clear niche (one day MMA, the next comedy, politics or conspiracies about the pyramids). Shaan's read is that the show is simply his tastes and interests pushed out for the world to see.
- **A house-cleaning creator on TikTok:** makes millions of dollars and has millions of followers who watch her clean and organize her house. One video of her organizing a fridge got 17M views. To Shaan it looks like work, but she loves it and the internet lets her turn it into a career.

chunks.heading: Why being the best at your thing pays: the internet finds you
chunks.text:
- Shaan's claim: "If you become the best at anything - you get paid handsomely."
- Examples he gives: the best croissant maker in LA can make more than a hedge fund guy in NY, and the best pre-school teachers (Ms. Rachel, Blippi) make millions on YouTube.
- Mechanism: the internet lets the best people get found, and they get huge rewards.
- Implication: authentic enthusiasm is a distribution advantage. People who love the work show visible energy, which attracts customers and audiences (the trainer's waiting list, Rogan's audience).

chunks.heading: The career goal Shaan recommends
chunks.text:
- Stop optimizing for hard work or for finding a "good job". Find the product that is just you pushed out.
- His stated career goal, which he invites others to steal: "Get paid a King's ransom for something that I would do for free."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan argues founders shouldn't default to Elon as their north star; instead pick the career you actually admire. He admires creative polymaths like Ben Franklin and Jesse Itzler, and uses Scott Adams' "find the price and pay it" framing to list the habits that lifestyle demands.

chunks.heading: Choosing role models: Elon is the default north star, but Shaan wouldn't want his life
chunks.text:
- Many founders treat Elon Musk as the north star. Shaan agrees he is probably the GOAT of entrepreneurs: richest person in the world, most famous founder, and fearless about going after the biggest, hardest problems.
- He still says "I'd never want to be him." His reasons: Elon's family life is a mess, he neglects his health, and he lives a high-stress life.
- He frames it with a line he attributes to "some wise monk, probably": "One man's heaven is another man's hell."
- The question he asks instead: whose life and career do you look at and say "gimme one of those"? He says it's never an exact copy you want, but a useful guide.

chunks.heading: Shaan's role model type: the creative polymath
chunks.text:
Shaan admires creative polymaths, people who succeed across many unrelated fields. His first example is Ben Franklin:
- Science: invented bifocals and the Franklin stove.
- Media: built a successful newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette.
- Politics: founding father who helped write the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence.
- Business: ran the US postal system as CEO and made it efficient and profitable.
- Music: invented the glass armonica, which influenced composers like Mozart and Beethoven.

His summary: "Science, Media, Politics, Business, Music… what a legend."

chunks.heading: Modern example: Jesse Itzler
chunks.text:
Shaan's modern-day polymath is Jesse Itzler:
- Started as a white-boy rapper.
- Wrote famous jingles and won an Emmy.
- Entrepreneur: coconut water, a private jet company.
- Prolific runner and endurance athlete.
- Lived in a monastery with monks, and had David Goggins live in his house.
- Wrote a couple of great books.
- Married Sara Blakely, has 4-5 kids, and seems like a good dad.

The appeal is a career that is wide and also seems to include a good family life, which is the part Shaan finds missing in the Elon model.

chunks.heading: Why this career shape appeals: "ride all the rides"
chunks.text:
- Shaan thinks it's because part of him feels life is short. His image: "Disneyland will close soon and I wanna ride all the rides before we get kicked out."
- The goal is breadth of experience across many domains rather than maximizing a single metric like net worth or company size.

chunks.heading: The price of the polymath path
chunks.text:
- He cites Scott Adams (creator of Dilbert): "If you want to be successful, find out what the price is and then pay it."
- Looking at his examples, the price Shaan wrote down for himself:
  - Reinvent yourself and not be afraid to start from scratch (beginner's mind).
  - Become a very quick learner.
  - Be unafraid to do things you're clueless at.
  - Be willing to change your career label, friend circle, and habits every few years.
- He says these all sound fun and sound like who he wants to be.

chunks.heading: The exercise to run
chunks.text:
- Pick your own "Elon": the person whose life you'd actually want, not just the most successful one.
- Use them as a guide rather than an exact copy.
- Work out what it costs (Scott Adams's "price"), write it down, and check whether paying it sounds fun to you. His closing question: "who's your Elon?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan answers reader questions. He shares what getting close to a margin call in the COVID crash taught him about leverage, selling, and doing nothing in a downturn. He also lays out how he reads, after Naval's idea that reading is about sparking thoughts, not collecting information.

chunks.heading: Holding through a market crash: leverage, patience, and selling early
chunks.text:
Shaan describes the nausea of a market crash: "There's a unique nausea that comes from losing 20% of your net worth over breakfast."

- After selling his first company to Twitch (owned by Amazon), he received a chunk of Amazon stock.
- Rich acquaintances advised "don't sell your stock, just borrow against it": hold the stock and still get liquid cash. The catch is a margin call if the stock crashes.
- He built an Excel calculator and found he could borrow ~60% of his stock and stay safe from a margin call unless something extreme happened.
- The pandemic then hit, and he came very close to a margin call. He was so stressed he "basically margin called" himself: he sold some stock, paid off the margin loan, and slept well, despite having lost about 30% of his net worth overnight.

chunks.heading: Three lessons from a crash
chunks.text:
1. "Leverage is like botox. Use with caution. Too much of it will f*ck your face up."
2. When a market crash happens, "respond, don't react." His rule is to do nothing for 30 days.
3. The most costly mistakes come from selling early, not buying wrong. A bad purchase caps your loss at 1x your investment. Selling early can cost you 2-10x of upside.

chunks.heading: Reading Naval's way: reading as a spark, not information intake
chunks.text: Shaan's favorite under-the-radar Naval line: "Reading isn't about putting information in your mind. Reading is about sparking a fire in your mind." He aims it at people who listen to podcasts at 2X or brag about how many books they read in a year. His view: the point of books is sparking new thoughts, not collecting info. Reading is to the brain what exercise is to the body.

chunks.heading: Shaan's three reading habits
chunks.text:
1. **Read a wide range.** He follows a management book with *Chimpanzee Politics* (power and sex among apes). Unrelated books spark new combinations of ideas.
2. **Reread the best stuff.** Rather than only reading new books, he rereads good ones several years later. He's a different person, so he takes something different from the same book. He cites the quote: "No man steps in the same river twice, for it is not the same river and he is not the same man."
3. **Pause while reading.** Speed reading is a mistake. If the goal is to spark a fire in your mind, "that fire needs air to breathe."

He also quits boring books: "There is no honor in finishing a bad book." He calls himself a "strategic quitter," which he says makes reading more fun and interesting.

chunks.heading: Reading the OpenAI departures (August 2024)
chunks.text:
Shaan says OpenAI "is starting to smell fishy" like a midwest sushi restaurant, and admits "I don't get it."

- Signals he lists: the top 2 safety leaders (Ilya Sutskever, Jan Leike) left, and the CTO was reported on "extended personal leave" (he names Greg, as written in the source).
- Co-founder John Schulman leaving for Anthropic, the nearest competitor, is highly unusual. His analogy: the Uber co-founder joining Lyft.
- His two hypotheses:
  - **Safety:** people joined for the mission of safe AGI, and the safety people are leaving because they think Sam is prioritizing winning and profit over safety first.
  - **Money:** people may be vesting out and getting huge offers at competitors, making it financially irresponsible to stay. OpenAI burning ~$5B a year in cash could be a worry, but he doubts it's the concern because "the size of the prize is too big."
- He says he doesn't know what is going on, but it will make a great Netflix doc in about 5 years.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Shaan answers reader questions on how to train a bias for action (treat it as a skill, get reps, notice wins, and change the questions you ask yourself). He also pitches an untried angel strategy of flipping seed investments at the next round, shares what he took from Twitch/Amazon (big companies are mediocre inside, writing memos matter), and gives his own definition of AGI.

chunks.heading: Bias for action is a trainable skill built from reps, noticing, and better prompts
chunks.text:
Shaan argues that a high action bias can be taught, but only if you first believe it is a skill rather than an inborn trait. He compares it to a player having a "motor" in sports: someone who just keeps moving and taking action, and he thinks the idea applies to every area of life.

His four-step method:
- **Believe it's a skill.** If you think it's a trait you're born with, you can't train it.
- **Get reps in small, safe places first.** He says "quit my job to start the company" shouldn't be the first bold action you ever take. Example: when you have an idea to improve your home office, grab the keys, drive to Home Depot, buy the parts, watch YouTube, and hammer it out in one night.
- **Pause to notice each time you act.** Awareness is a "superpower." When you pick up the phone and call instead of procrastinating, or lace up shoes and walk instead of being tired, take note, so your brain reinforces "there's more evidence of me having an insanely high action bias."
- **Change your factory settings.** See the next section.

chunks.heading: Rewrite the questions you ask your brain to get faster, bigger answers
chunks.text:
Shaan treats his brain like ChatGPT: you put in a prompt and it spits out an answer. Rather than trying to make the AI smarter, "it's much easier to try just changing the prompt first."

- His default questions in a situation were "what should I do?" and "will this work?" He calls these weak questions.
- Better questions: "how can I take massive action on this idea?" and "how can I move with speed on this?"
- Adding words like "massive action" and "move with speed" makes the brain "come up with a completely different answer."

chunks.heading: Flipping as an untried early-stage investing strategy
chunks.text:
Asked for the investing equivalent of basketball's three-pointer discovery, Shaan says edges like this are hard to find and offers a "half baked" answer: **flipping**. Real estate has both buy-and-hold investors and flippers, but tech investing only has buy-and-hold.

- As an angel investor he makes many bets and waits about 10 years hoping 1-2 become multi-billion dollar winners.
- His estimate is that more than 50% of his seed bets raise another round, at an average valuation increase of roughly 2.5-3X (he says he'd have to run the numbers).
- Illustrative math: 10 investments at $100k each; 60% raise a new round at a 3X increase and are sold. That turns $1M into $1.8M (80%), usually in under 2 years, about a 34% IRR, which he says would outperform 95% of venture funds with far more liquidity.
- Bonus for founders: if the seed investor sells to the new investor, the founder takes less net dilution.
- Why nobody does it: **perception**. Angels are supposed to be true believers who hold to exit or IPO, but "those are just cultural norms, not rules." It's the one tech-investing strategy he'd love to see someone try.

chunks.heading: What he took from the inside of Amazon
chunks.text:
Shaan clarifies that he sold his first company to Twitch (owned by Amazon), not Amazon directly, and was there about 2 years. He says it was like spending a summer in Bezos' pool house, not the main house. Two takeaways:

- **Big companies aren't as sophisticated as they look.** He had assumed his scrappy startups were doing things the dumb way and big tech must be sophisticated inside. He found some impressive things but "mostly a zoo of mediocrity."
- **Writing culture is the best habit he kept.** Writing memos forces clarity of thought and is the best way to communicate inside companies. He still uses the Amazon 6-page memo.

chunks.heading: Why names matter and the Uncle Shaan nickname
chunks.text:
Shaan believes "names matter," pointing to Whoopi Goldberg, who he says wouldn't have been as successful as Caryn Johnson.

- He tried to self-assign a nickname ("Shaan The Don," "Shanny J," "LL Cool Shaan," then "Shaan P," like Gary V). It flopped; nobody used it.
- "Uncle Shaan" stuck only when a friend, George, suggested a YouTube channel where people call in with questions for Uncle Shaan, and other friends started saying it.
- His aim is to be "the internet's fun rich uncle."
- Lesson: "don't try to give yourself a nickname, that's not how it works."

chunks.heading: AGI definitions and his own test
chunks.text:
Shaan says the common expert definition is "when computers are as smart as the smartest humans at a wide range of cognitive tasks," meaning expert level at pretty much everything humans can do. But the definition keeps changing and nobody agrees.

- The Turing test was once the milestone, and AI has now passed it with "nobody freaking out."
- **His definition:** AGI is the point when AI is better at developing AI than humans. At that point AI improves exponentially without human involvement.
- He sees open questions after that: whether it stays a tool or develops its own agenda, and what stops a human from using it for evil.
- He relays an investor friend (ex-Peter Thiel) saying "GLP > GPT," meaning Ozempic is a bigger deal than ChatGPT, and says you should be more scared of gaining 25 lbs than of AGI.

chunks.heading: Ozempic as "cheating" and the status-symbol question
chunks.text:
Shaan is "100% Team Ozempic-Is-Cheating." People are free to take it, but he can't give the same respect he gives someone who works hard and disciplines mind and body to lose weight, versus someone taking a shot every 2 weeks.

- He asks what becomes the new status symbol if losing weight gets easy. In the Victorian era, with scarce food, everyone was skinny and being fat was the status symbol.
- He jokes he hopes society returns to the Roman era, when a huge nose was considered masculine and attractive.

I just hired a new CEO for one of my companies. On Day 1 - he started doing what most CEO’s would do:

- Meet & greet the team

Nat was named CEO of Github, and what he did on Day 1 was amazing.

[8 am: everyone in the company gets on a call].

Instead of sharing the vision & multi-year plan. Nat screen-shared and displayed a giant list of 100+ issues & complaints from customers.

He said: “Today, we’re going to find one item on here, and fix it”

“And tomorrow, we’re going to pick another one, and fix that”

“And the next day.. And the next.. Until we’ve nailed 20+ of these”

This did 3 big things:

1) Shock Therapy. The team used to “think in quarters and years”. Suddenly the timeline shrinks to “ship something today”.

2) Taught Him The Business, Bottoms Up. Where are the problems? Where’s the tech debt? Which teams are good at getting shit done?

3) Action Speaks Louder. Customers were worried when Microsoft bought GitHub. Will they ruin it? Should we leave? But immediately seeing the product improve built faith that things will be OK.

I call this the ‘Broken Shelf Approach’.

Every home has broken shelves. The people living in the house have learned to ignore it, and just live with it.

If you want to make an impression when you move in. Find the broken shelves, and fix them first.

"Why did Chipotle (and 11 other restaurant chains) ALL start in Colorado?"

I'll tell you the answer, but first, a story. 

(hint - it's the same reason movies come from hollywood and big tech companies are in silicon valley. )

I'll explain with a quick story.

When I was 21, my first business idea was to create the "Chipotle of Sushi".

we didn't know anything about the restaurant business - so we just did something so dumb, that it was smart (the midwit meme).

I asked, "if we're building the chipotle of sushi, why don't we launch where chipotle launched?"

quick google -- denver colorado.

Random right?

Maybe not. Turns out that a sh*tload of restaurant chains started in colorado.

Qdoba, Quiznos, Noodles & Company, Smashburger, Madgreens, Larkburger, all started in colorado.

And other chains like Einstein's bagels, Boston Market, and the one and only Macaroni Grill all have their headquarters in Colorado.

Because that's where all the fast-casual talent is.

This is because of a concept called:  "Talent Density". 

It's very simple, but often overlooked. 

By moving to denver: 
- our lawyer was the same lawyer who setup Chipotle's franchise agreements 
- our real estate agent helped them roll out their first 200 locations 
- our menu designer was the same one that standardized their recipes

They all live there.

We didn't have to waste time figuring things out. We could steal 80% of their existing playbook, and change 20% for our specific needs.  

Same thing in Silicon Valley. 

Paypal birthed a group of talented people - who then went on to start SpaceX, Yelp, YouTube, LinkedIn, Tesla, etc..

Talent density is when a bunch of people who have super specific, unique skills (eg. movie production, coding apps, or investing in commodities) all live in one area.

They get smarter, faster, and hop from "hot company" to hot company again and again, compounding their advantage.

(sidebar: this is why it's idiotic when people move away from california to lower their tax rate. They save 13% on taxes but lose the talent density and 10X opportunities that come with it)

@JamesCurrier sat me down and told me: "you want to be as close to the white HOT CENTER of the network as possible."

So the highest +EV decision you can make as a young, ambitious person is to move to the absolute GEOGRAPHIC CENTER of your field.

And if you're building an empire, build it where the empire builders live, you'll recruit better talent, faster.

For movies, go to hollywood. For finance, go to wall street. For tech, come to SF.

3 ways to hijack the creative part of your brain: 

1. Morning Mud 

we mistakenly think greatness is clean. 

Like  you're supposed to wake up, meditate, cold plunge, sip green tea -- and then produce brilliant work. 

Nope. 

You gotta work like a pig. Wake up, and roll in the mud. 

Seinfeld spent the first 2 hours of his day writing jokes. Why? because if you want great jokes, you gotta write a lot of bad jokes. 

He did that everyday, for 40+ years. Less than 0.1% of those jokes ever made it into his standup set. 

Quantity is the mother of quality. 

b..bu..buut what about writer's block? 

"there's no writers block" he said. "there IS scared. there IS lazy. But there's no writers block."

You can cure writers block like it's a simple case of the hiccups: "just sit down and accept your mediocrity"

Translation: the harder you try to be great, the more you paralyze your creativity. Instead, be willing to roll in the mud. Make bad stuff, everyday. 

Ed Sheeran: "I don't try to be great. When I walk in the studio, I remind myself 'today, I must dare to suck'...you can never make a great song, if you're afraid to make a bad song"

The first 2 hours of the day. Sit down and create. 

Before you check the news, twitter, and stock market. BEFORE YOU PUT ANYTHING IN YOUR BRAIN... make something. 

Coders code. Writers write. Musicians play music.

You will only be as great as you're willing to be bad.

If you're reading this - you work too much, and it's suffocating your creativity. 

All great work is on the other side of a breakthru idea.

"Creativity is just connecting things" - Steve Jobs

Einstein used to float on a boat without a motor at sea. The coast guard was worried he'd drift away. He said "good, more time to think"

JK Rowling came up with Harry Potter on a train.

If I had to compress one important idea I've learned about podcasting, it would be this: 

"notice what you have an contagious irrational passion for -- and bottle it up for the rest of us"

Contagious, irrational passion. 

If your interest level is rational...you're not gonna make it.

Irrational is you fall asleep listening to old talks on youtube about it. You read everything you can get your hands on. You care about it far beyond it's usefulness to you. 

Contagious is also important. You know how some people's laugh makes you laugh, even when the joke isn't funny to you? You need that as a creator. Your passion must be so contagious that you get me excited about stuff I don't even care about. I watched a youtube documentary yesterday on the best scrabble player in the world. 

5 minutes before that, I didn't care. But 5 minutes into it, I was hooked. The guys excitement about this scrabble god was contagious. 

Most people don't have anything they're irrationally, contagiously passionate about. That's fine. Most people don't need/deserve to have a popular channel. 

But I suspect many more people could have one, than currently do. That's because most people underestimate themselves. They think they need some special skill or experience. Nope. 

And even if you do notice it, most people lack courage to actually go for it. They're so afraid to fail, they will instead will try to fit for what they're guessing people want. No no no. bad bad dumb dumb. 

Gotta own what you nerd out about.

Not everybody has contagious irrational passion, but if you do -- don't underestimate it. 

You can  tap dance to work everyday, and make hundreds of millions of dollars as a byproduct. 

Bill Simmons has an irrational, contagious passion for sports & pop culture. For 20 years he's been podcasting & blogging about it with his friends.
